«Her Institute was founded principally for the sick in their homes, then for endangered girls, for the poorest, then for hospitals, for orphans, for prisoners, in short for every sort of misery.

In doing temporal good to neighbor, the Servant of God wished to arrive at her principal aim of saving souls. When she was invited and had personnel available, she did not look at the economic conditions proposed to her, but sent her daughters at once, after agreement with the Bishops, trusting for the rest in Providence. When she sent her daughters to Florence, she sent them unprovided with everything, and when they came to Rome accompanied by the Servant of God, they were so unprovided that they had to make do sleeping on the floor [...]. The Servant of God slept on two chairs.

Finding her sisters afflicted or worried, she at once comforted and consoled them. At her words anxiety, sadness, doubt vanished, and we were all left serene. This I know, not only from my personal experience, but also because it was reported to me by other sisters.

Her solicitude to console her religious extended to every kind of tribulation; and I know that sometimes she handed money to some religious to have Masses celebrated in suffrage for the souls of their loved ones. She exhorted us all to mutual charity, and if, despite her remarks, she saw that some dissension persisted among sisters, she assigned them to other houses and so separated them.

I never heard that the Servant of God complained of anyone. Not even once when three of our sisters, who were in a hospital entrusted to us, refused to remain subject to our Foundress and, having changed habit, continued to remain in that hospital, not even then, I say, did the Servant of God complain. Her words followed upon deeds, and she exhorted us all not to bear rancor toward those who had offended and persecuted us, and to continue, if possible, to do them good.

She did not want her daughters, and to this she exhorted them, to envy other Institutes that had an aim similar to ours, and she inculcated in us that we should pray that God would make them prosper, saying that none of this should matter to us, provided God be glorified.

Her charity extended still to the poor departed, and we have prescribed by the Servant of God for them some daily prayers. When the Servant of God sent us to assist the sick in their homes, she exhorted us to take care to comfort the family of the sick person.

She gave much alms to the poor, in clothes (as at Piacenza), in bread, in soup, and also in money especially in winter. For them she also worked. From the time she was a layperson, and then as a religious, she went begging for the poor, for the sick, and to be able to send the obolus to the Holy Father [...]. Until she was prevented by the government of her Institute, which expanded very rapidly, she did not spare herself in going personally to assist the sick, for whom I know she felt great inclination.

The Servant of God did not want anything ever to be expected as compensation for the service rendered to the sick, not even a cup of coffee, she only allowed a glass of water to be taken [...]. When the Servant of God corrected her religious, she never raised her voice, and woe to that superior who threatened her subjects, and she wanted them to be calm when they had to rebuke. I never knew of any religious being badly impressed or irritated by the corrections of the Servant of God, and it seems to me I can affirm with all certainty that she knew how to regulate her words of correction according to the character of those to whom they were addressed»

180. 66. — The panorama of Mother Rosa's love for neighbor offered us by the Most Eminent Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, is also very complete:

«To the charity of God so ardent in her heart, there responded, as a perfect echo, charity for neighbor. Proof of it is the foundation of her Institute, wholly devoted to the care of neighbor, indeed it has as a means of sanctification the care of the neighbor in body and morals.

I now recall a small episode, which was reported to me by the religious themselves. The Servant of God having arrived on the occasion of her visits at a hospital run by her daughters, and no comfortable place being found for her to rest, she set herself to assist a dying woman, and stayed at her bedside until death. When that poor woman died, the corpse was removed, and the Servant of God, not minding that she had died of plague, and not even asking that the bed linen be changed, lay down in that same bed and slept there.

It happened sometimes that — having known by supernatural light that some of her religious were not completely at peace with God — in the admonitions and corrections she gave them, she did not expose them to the disesteem of others, but gave them privately, opening their eyes to their spiritual state with great charity and generally with happy result [...].

She prayed much for sinners and mortified herself with harsh penances. To those who asked her for prayers, having trust in her, she did not refuse them. The Servant of God took a personal interest that at the door of the houses of the Institute, in which she found herself, care be taken to give alms to the poor who presented themselves.

By the offenses others did to her she did not feel touched; she received them out of love of the Lord; it is therefore not even a case of asking whether she forgave them. Most devout to the souls in purgatory, she suffraged them with her prayers, with penances, and also with Mass alms [...].

p. 78

As a complement of her charity, I will say that the Servant of God never failed in the forms of kindness and courtesy due on occasion of visits of outsiders, and also with her subordinates. When, however, in her conversations on visits the talk became vain or frivolous, one saw that she remained absorbed in higher thoughts and became a stranger to the conversation»181.

Although very brief, it is for us very interesting to report here the testimony of the Capuchin, Fr. Vincenzo da Alatri, chaplain at the convent of the Conception in Rome and confessor of the community of the generalate house:

«Of charity toward neighbor the Servant of God had so much. And this was toward the bashful poor whom she helped with many considerations. I heard from the sisters that she helped not only with money, but also with food and clothing. At the solemnities of Easter and above all at Christmas she distributed pasta and sausages, besides the usual bread, and I too saw it with my own eyes, and I was amazed at the great quantity. She naturally helped first of all the poorest houses. Her charity toward the sick is already revealed by the foundation of her Institute; but moreover she took every care for her sick daughters, and wanted them to be treated very well»182.

67. — Also very significant is the deposition of Mons. Carlo Amirante, witness XIX at the Naples Process:

«As regards charity toward neighbor, whether for the spirit or for the body, the Servant of God reached true and proper sacrifice. I am truly witness of how she strove, when things came to her knowledge, to eliminate even possible improprieties: and through an undeserved trust in me, when she supposed that some sister was either troubled in conscience or in danger, she referred her to me and ipso facto, without regard for commitments, administrators or influential persons, she removed her and moved her elsewhere. And sometimes she said to me: ‘Charity is ordered first to the interests of eternity, then to those of time. The greatest evil, indeed the only evil, is sin’. She in fact provided and took care with commitment that spiritual helps should not be lacking in the houses: and it was for this that it fell to me to travel a good part of Italy, always, however, with the consent of my superiors.

Love of the poor, of the suffering, of the unhappy, was the counselor of the work of the Servant of God. And this love, it is my conviction, she learned from the open wounds of her dear Crucified. She did not tolerate comparisons between Institute and Institute; she was content with the little that could be done, as she said, the increase belongs to God. She suffered oppositions, almost torments, because of the movements that the Institute itself gave in its branches: and I having allowed myself sometimes to sympathize with her, I had in reply: ‘The poor suffer so much!’, and when I saw her at the bedside of dying sisters, her soul was turned to God and she thanked Him that another daughter was transplanted to heaven.

p. 79

I know that she loved her slanderers and, since she was obliged to deal with me on some family questions and also concerning the rules of the Institute, no word of resentment ever escaped her mouth, and when things were most evident, she said to me: ‘Professor, but let us pray for our opponents: do not forget that Jesus forgave his crucifiers from the cross’»183.

From the deposition of the brother of the Servant of God, Francesco Gattorno, witness II at the Genoa Process, we glean the following very brief passages, which will help us understand ever better Mother Rosa's love for neighbor:

«Before being placed in marriage she was like the soul of the paternal home. I recall [...] that she, with an activity and self-denial worthy of every praise, discharged for the most part the domestic offices, devoting to these all the time, deducting that in which she attended to her own instruction.

My mother suffered from frequent attacks of suffocation; the sister immediately younger than Rosa was frail, also following a surgical operation in which she was assisted by Rosa; the other sister was still very small. Besides, the maternal grandmother was in the house, in need of continual assistance because of age; and we were also in the house two brothers younger than she and the eldest, and therefore she had to bear continual and heavy work. This she sustained without any complaint, with an admirable diligence, so that everything in the house proceeded in order, nothing was lacking to anyone and, especially with the old grandmother and then infirm until death, with mother in her sufferings, with the frailer sister and with all of us she lavished the most loving care. So her departure from the family was for it a grave loss.

She distinguished herself by her spirit of charity; she loved to make directly herself certain distributions to the poor customary in the family; all she could dispose of she gave to the needy, and especially at the ‘bocchetta di S. Francesco d’Albaro’, where the family went to the country, she was sought out by all for her charity. Even afterward, and for many years, they asked me, gratefully, for news of her»184.

The same witness, brother of the Servant of God, recalls those difficult moments in which uncle Federico Campanella, brother of the mother, an intimate follower of Giuseppe Mazzini, gathered at home with Masons and unbelieving and atheist comrades-in-arms. Many times the Servant of God met with them and this was a reason for her to practice charity heroically.

«My brother Federico too — the witness testifies — fought among the Garibaldians and Mazzinians, and was a colonel of the General Staff of Giuseppe Garibaldi. For this reason my sister Rosa had to meet several times with personages of the party opposed to hers, who came to our house. She never yielded in matters of ideas, but by the sincerity of her faith, the delicacy of her manner and the goodness she showed in everything, she won from them too an unlimited esteem»185.

68. — For political reasons Federico, brother of Mother Rosa, was imprisoned in the prisons of Alessandria in the Bormida fortress, and the Servant of God did not fail to visit him, carried by her great charity:

«My sister ran from Piacenza to Alessandria and, by her quality as mother of the nurses of St. Anne, she was able to be the first to penetrate the prison and bring the comforts of the case to the political detainees. This increased esteem for Rosa and won her the gratitude also of the advanced parties»186.

Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, witness III at the Roman Process, confesses that, seeing the Mother's charity toward the sick, she would have «wished to have some small illness in order to be assisted by her»:

«Her love for neighbor made her take good care of the sick. And she was so delicate in assisting that I myself would have wished to have some small illness in order to be assisted by her. She exhorted us too to assist the sick well, and to do good to their souls, and she showed herself wholly glad on learning that some conversion of these sick people was being worked.

Great was her charity toward us, for when we were not in full observance, she also inspired fear in us, but she was wholly amiable when we had nothing to reproach ourselves with. She wanted superiors to treat the sisters very well, especially if sick. On some feasts she had us served something extra at table, or else during recreation she herself distributed sweets, and so gave a quite special tone of cheerfulness to the feast»187.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, reveals to us very significant details concerning the charity of the Servant of God:

«The Servant of God occupied herself with children when she was still a young girl, and always occupied herself with them also when she lived in the world. From then on she strove to have First Communion made, especially by those boys and girls who had passed the usual age for that act. When she knew some needy youth who wished to become a priest, she herself helped him as best she could, and recommended him to others for help. And this she always did throughout her life. She always helped other young people of poor family to put them in a position to obtain a job, a trade. I recall the particular case of a young man who was helped by her, and so was able to obtain his degree as a lawyer.

She occupied herself very much with little orphan girls to place them in some institute; she therefore also provided them with a small trousseau, and if there was no way to obtain free entry into the institute, she herself procured a small monthly subsidy. The sisters who turned to her uncertain, doubtful, agitated, were completely reassured by the Servant of God and left her room content [...]. I saw several persons who no longer wanted to know of God or Church, who came to the Servant of God and who were by her led back to Jesus; she always had some in hand, and used to say: ‘We must make more account of these strayed persons than of those who walk by themselves on the right road, and we must take greater care of them, so the Lord wills’. She prayed and had prayers made not only in general for sinners, but also in particular for this one or that, and had Communions offered for them by her sisters too. She then also took an interest in their perseverance and inquired by sometimes sending sisters to get news. She also inculcated in the sisters, especially the superiors, that they should occupy themselves with poor sinners. When she had workmen in the house she called them to her and asked them all the particulars of their family, not only for the spiritual part, but also for the temporal part. She took a particular interest in their children, whether they had made First Communion, seeing that they made it. I recall that the brother-in-law of Princess Fitalia had abandoned God. The Princess did everything so that he would come to Rome to speak with the Servant of God. Although reluctantly he was induced, and the Servant of God drew him to the Lord. After continuing in the life of conversion, he died holy some years ago. Many others she led to the Lord by her work and her word. When she went to a hospital run by our sisters, she inquired whether there was some obstinate person who refused the sacraments, and then she set to work for their conversion and always succeeded. Sometimes these strayed patients were at first irritated by her exhortations and threw at her what was presented to them, such as a cup of broth, etc., but she was not offended, attributed the fact to their illness and returned to them with all gentleness and sweetness, until those unfortunates, attracted by her good manners, surrendered. Many of them then said to her: ‘It would be necessary for you, mother, to be always here with us’. And she comforted them assuring them that she would not abandon them»188.

69. — Charity informed the apostolic zeal of the Servant of God. Sr. A. Vittoria Archetti, witness IV at the Roman Process, testifies in this regard:

«Ardent was her zeal for the conversion of unbelievers and of sinners. She prayed and inculcated in us that we should pray for this purpose. For this same purpose she sent her sisters to America and to Africa. Before they left for these places she had them make the Spiritual Exercises and in taking leave of them she exhorted them so warmly to the work and to sacrifice, that one saw clearly how much faith and zeal she harbored in her heart»189.

p. 82

Sr. A. Cunegonda Pacini, witness VI at the Naples Process, attests:

«The Servant of God loved in God her neighbor, to whose relief she consecrated all her activity. Proof of this is the foundation of our Institute, which proposes, with the glory of God, also the spiritual and temporal good of neighbor. Before founding the Institute the Servant of God already loved to devote herself to the good of neighbor. She belonged to the pious Association of the Daughters of Mary in Genoa, occupying herself especially with the spiritual good of the poor and then also in Genoa with great love she frequented the hospitals, always seeking to be useful in assisting the poor sick and needy. It was certainly this love of neighbor one of the principal motives that induced her to found an institute that proposed especially help to the sick in private homes and in hospitals, and on the other hand to provide for the religious and civil instruction of girls and of the children of the people. She herself acted as teacher to the first sisters to train them for the catechetical teaching to be given to the children of the people, and in such teaching she was always an example and encouragement to the other sisters and recommended that this be practiced in all our houses»190.

Interesting is the brief mention of Sr. A. Margherita d’Arcangelo, witness XVIII at the Naples Process:

«She had a particular concern that the religious sentiment be preserved among the peoples and this was the principal aim of the foundation of our Institute. She inculcated in all of us her religious the sentiment of edifying neighbor by our good example and of cooperating so that sinners might return to God»191.

Sr. A. Michelina Negri, witness X at the Roman Process, confirms:

«She burned with desire for the conversion of unbelievers and of sinners and would have been ready, as she said, to give her blood for them. ‘Blessed she — she told us — who can convert a sinner, because she has assured the salvation of her own soul’. She prayed and exhorted us all to pray, also in our private prayers, for the conversion of unbelievers and sinners. She desired that her Institute be called to some mission among the unbelievers, as then happened. When then some band was to leave for these missions, she encouraged them with such accents that the sisters felt afterwards their soul full of sweetness and courage»192.

She showed great attention and delicacy toward endangered girls; so Sr. A. Apollonia Marchetti, witness VII at the Naples Process, recalls:

«The Servant of God was full of charity toward neighbor, whom she loved exclusively for love of God. The works instituted by her are works eminently of charity, such as free assistance to the sick, and the asylum for poor endangered little orphans. Personally she went to the sick, to whom she gave her assistance; many times of sick girls, in need of care, she took them on her lap, dressed their wounds, cleaned them and kept them sheltered in the orphanage»193.

Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, witness III at the Roman Process, adds:

«When at Piacenza we had orphan or endangered girls, she herself sometimes went to assist them, when she knew them to be ill. A certain Sr. Anna Beatrice of the Piacenza house told me that when she was still a pupil in that house she fell gravely ill with typhus and that the Servant of God spent long hours at her bedside and sometimes whole nights»194.

B. CARDINAL VIRTUES

70. — The heights of grace and holiness illustrated in the preceding chapter should find confirmation in the examination of the exercise of the four virtues of Prudence, Justice, Fortitude and Temperance, which preside more directly over the regulation and balance of man's concrete activity. It would not, in fact, profit much to have illustrated and shown the richness of the supernatural life of Mother Rosa Gattorno, enriched with so many and such singular charisms, if we then did not find in her operations, in her daily life, also an adequate excellence in the exercise of these virtues, which are the hinges of Christian and human life.

Now, the first and fundamental consideration to be made in this regard is that, far from having remained, so to speak, burrowed in her ivory tower as a privileged soul, Mother Rosa had a busy and dynamic life, according to the demands of her vocation and of her state in its different phases of daughter of a family, wife, mother and widow, religious and foundress of an Institute of consecrated life. Indeed, we can affirm that abstraction, ecstasy, contemplation rather accentuated, but purifying it and making it more effective and shrewd, her external activity.

1. Prudence

71. — It is a corollary of all that has been set forth thus far that the Servant of God distinguished herself in all the phases of her life: childhood, adolescence, youth, marriage, widowhood and religious life, in orienting existence to the ultimate end, in harmoniously regulating her choices according to the demands of the Christian vocation and in harmony with perfection. This aspect is rather plain from the whole of her life. And the means she put into practice: assiduous prayer, habitual frequentation of the sacraments, spirit of mortification, flight from occasions, industriousness, commitments of apostolate, etc., stand as confirmation of the supernatural prudential criterion of the Servant of God.

Rather, it is necessary to highlight her peculiar criteria of human and supernatural prudence especially in her life as Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne and as Superior General of the Institute founded by her. Here the testimonies are of considerable incisiveness, because they bring out an excellent habit of sagacity, of penetration, of balance of government both in material things and especially in spiritual ones. Thus the witnesses observe her capacity of judgment and her peculiar wisdom in the various decisions to be taken. But here are some testimonies as proof.

Already from her earliest age Mother Rosa «always gave proof of good sense and of maturity of judgment», and so it appears from the deposition of Sr. A. Apollonia Marchetti, witness VIII at the Naples Process:

«Prudence shone admirably throughout the life of the Servant of God. For the time in which she lived in the world and was a young girl, then wife, then mother, as far as I have learned from persons of her family, and above all from her mother, she always gave proof of good sense, of maturity of judgment, and above all of exemplariness of life and of edifying exactness in the fulfillment of all her duties. Having become then Foundress and Superior of our religious community, she always let herself be admired for irreproachable conduct, for religious observance, for the way she governed her dependents who always held her as a providential mother. She was most watchful in the choice and admission of novices, in the assignment of individuals to the various offices, and in providing for the good running of the communities and of the works entrusted to her. Also in preventing and correcting inconveniences and abuses, she always gave proof of watchfulness, of discretion and of truly admirable judgment: and it is a fact that never, as far as I know, was a disorder deplored that could be charged to a lack of prudence on her part. All this I depose for what is known to me, and for what I have learned in the community. And from the whole of the information I have on the matter, I have formed the judgment that her prudence was not human, but proceeded from a much higher principle; nor ever, as far as is known to me, did she transgress the just limits of Christian prudence»195.

Of this good sense and maturity of judgment of the Mother Sr. A. Amante La Barbera, witness XXXVIII, ex officio, at the Roman Process, also bears witness:

«All her actions she directed to God, as appeared from her conversation and her works. The principal means she used to obtain the eternal salvation of others were prayers and works of charity. She was never heard, as far as I know, to take part in or make talk that was either light or of little usefulness. I know, in general, that she took counsel before deciding something important, either with Bishops, or with other wise persons, and as I said in another session, she prayed. She never showed liking or dislike for any of her daughters. I know from my own personal experience that the Mother used much tact with her little daughters: sometimes she yielded to their reluctances so as not to dishearten and disconcert them, and by all she was esteemed as very prudent. In spending she was neither prodigal nor tight [...]. Confiding in the Servant of God, we were perfectly tranquil, because we knew that whatever we had deposited in her heart, never came out again, without our needing to ask her to keep it to herself»196

72. — Evident proof of this great prudence of the Servant of God is the following testimony of her great friend and confidante the Princess of Fitalia, witness XXXI, ex officio at the Roman Process:

«To me she said: ‘One must never do anything without asking counsel’, and she added that I should ask counsel also of several persons. As to her spiritual direction she once said to me: ‘The Lord has given to all, and even to the saints, a guide (and she cited St. Teresa) and to me the Lord has not granted so much grace; but now I go to confession to the Father General of the Minors, and I receive so much consolation, because he understands me completely’. A year later she added still: ‘The Lord now permits that he no longer understand me, and it is a most painful trial!’. Now I recall that she said that besides asking counsel, one must pray. She gave me counsels with such humility that I had to ask her for them; the results then were such that they persuaded me that she was enlightened from above.

I always saw her so occupied that I sometimes felt scruples about stealing a little of her time, although my soul received so much benefit from it and felt so great a need. She was, one may say, crushed by work; but in all this business I saw well that her union with God never ceased. I believe that she dispatched her correspondence largely at night, as I know from her herself»197.

We take from Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, the following very significant words regarding the prudence of Mother Rosa:

«The Servant of God was very prudent, spoke little and measured; with grave and concentrated bearing. She was very secretive, and when someone confided something to her, there was no chance she would let anything leak. When she received letters of praise and commendations for herself or for her work, she said: ‘These are things that do not concern us; the work is the Lord's’. I remember that a certain gentleman one day said to me and to Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega words of praise for our Institute, and revealed the fine qualities of our Mother. I was greatly delighted, and in the evening, accompanying the Servant of God to her room, I had the imprudence to say to her: ‘Mother, but do you not know that this and that is said of you?’. And she: ‘Oh! my poor daughter! What are you saying? The work is the Lord's, I am nothing but his donkey’. And these words she said with so much sincerity and frankness that I was edified [...].

When she had something important to decide, she strongly recommended us to pray and I saw her in those days more recollected than usual, and more than usual she used scraps of time to go to the chapel or her room. In the gravest cases she also had the Most Blessed Sacrament exposed for some hours of the day, and sent us to pray.

In the most important matters she took counsel with prudent persons, such as with Fr. Bernardino da Portogruaro and, when he was no longer in Rome, with Mons. Belmonte, now Cardinal, and for daily and ordinary matters with Fr. Agostino Donadio. I have also heard it said that in the first years she took much counsel with Fr. Tornatore, a priest of the Mission [...]. It is her example that taught us to hold the general councils and the other chapters for the more important matters»198.

73. — A moment in which she manifested better than ever the great prudence that was characteristic of her was that of the visits to the different houses of the Institute as Superior General and Foundress of it. On these visits and on the exquisite prudence with which she carried them out, we have many testimonies, all firsthand and from persons who knew the Servant of God closely for many years. So Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, expresses herself:

«She frequently visited, every one or two years, the houses of the Institute in Italy, and where she did not go, as in America, she sent Visitors, and demanded of the Superiors a report on the economic and disciplinary running of the houses. Following the visits she took the measures judged most opportune and necessary without regard for anyone. In the visits, as I myself was able to see once, accompanying her to one of these houses in Genoa, she first received the subjects and then the superiors. Once the Servant of God was ill and the secretary and the assistants tried to dissuade her from the visit she wanted to make to our houses in Sicily; and making use of the familiarity that the Servant of God granted me with her, they said to me: ‘You too must try to dissuade the Mother from this visit to Sicily, and persuade her to have the superior come to Rome’. Then I went to the Servant of God, pointing out to her that the aim of the visit would be obtained equally, sparing herself while ill and having the superior come to Rome. And the Servant of God: ‘You are right, my daughter, that I should spare myself, but if I go there I can hear both subjects and superiors and know the true state of things. If I call the superiors to Rome, they will tell me what I already know’, and she went off with fever»199.

74. — She was always held to be a wise and most prudent Superior, even if it is true that ‘during her long term of 35 years as superior general there was no lack of difficult moments of grave contrarieties and sorrows. Very eloquent in this respect is the deposition of Sr. A. Maristella Calderone, witness I at the Naples Process:

«Holy prudence shone constantly in the life of the Servant of God, in the way she regulated herself, aiming at her own sanctification and knowing how to choose the best part, and in the irreproachable manner in which she governed the community dependent on her. It is a fact that nothing was ever found to criticize, as far as I know, in the dispositions issued by her, in the way she handled both the foundation and the running of the Institute; she always knew how to overcome all difficulties, and never gave rise to disturbances or positive dissensions among her dependents. She was generally held by all of us as a wise and enlightened woman, and we always turned to her in all things both of the work and of our individual circumstances, and we always found ourselves well in following her counsels; a word from her sufficed to dispel all doubts and to resolve all difficulties. Great prudence the Servant of God always showed in correcting: she was strong and energetic and did not permit abuses, indeed she knew how to prevent in time every least disorder; but her prudence and charity made it so that no one remained offended or pained by the correction received, since besides the gentle and insinuating way in which she knew how to season the rebuke, she also had the foresight to hide from those to whom it was not needful to reveal it the fault or defect of the others: correction was always made with charity and discretion and with the greatest possible secrecy»200.

Sr. A. Vittoria Archetti, witness IV at the Roman Process, speaks to us again with praise of the wisdom of the Mother in the government of the Institute:

«As far as I know, she always sent as superiors to the houses the most observant, prudent and most suitable religious. Toward her sisters she showed herself truly a loving mother, and wanted also that all the superiors should show themselves such toward their subjects. And I recall that in the letters addressed to me, she not only exhorted me to firm maintenance of discipline, but also to show myself good toward the sisters of my house and to watch continually. She did not let herself in any decision be guided by likes or dislikes, she was no respecter of persons»201.

p. 88

75. — The Most Rev. Mons. Carlo Amirante, witness XIX, ex officio, at the Naples Process, alludes in this deposition of his to several other moments in Mother Rosa's life in which her prudence shone splendidly:

«I held the Servant of God in esteem as a most prudent woman: first because in the disagreements often occurring between her relatives and her work, she always smoothed them over in a tranquil manner [...]; second because in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, often exposed to slanders, to the oppositions of administrators, purveyors, etc., the Servant of God knew how to resolve things in such a way that all remained satisfied. She was sometimes content with the closing of some house so as not to expose her sisters to the possibility of calumnies and the like, as happened with the house at Nola and the house in the Ravaschieri hospice in Naples and also here in the hospital of the Pace. I also know that the Servant of God was slow to correct, because, not having first information, she always admonished with gentleness: when then she had assured herself of the existence of the evil, she punished severely without showing herself severe, and this I was able several times to verify through my continual relations with the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. I am sure that with such prudence the Servant of God showed herself adorned until death»202.

A measure of good government and of wisdom is the study of the characters of persons on the part of superiors and this is one of the dominant notes of the way in which Mother Rosa governed her Institute. In fact Sr. A. Michelina Negri, witness X at the Roman Process, expresses herself thus in this regard:

«She studied the characters of the sisters and knew how to take them on their own side. To the superiors she also recommended that they too study characters, and warned them that, while one could be taken with rigor, the other had to be taken with gentleness. ‘See — she said to them — in a ward there may be many sick, but the same medicines do not suit all alike: one must know how to adapt them’. There was no sister corrected by her who left her room offended, so well did she know how to make corrections»203.

76. — On Mother Rosa's prudence in the matter of the foundation and in her relations with her hierarchical superiors it suffices to listen to the voice of His Eminence Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process:

«The Servant of God, in taking measures and dispositions in the direction of her Institute, in the most difficult circumstances always turned to Jesus Christ, to St. Anne and to her holy Protectors, and did not carry out her steps and her measures except when she felt strongly assisted by supernatural aids. From this it followed that, when she was opposed by anyone, especially by Bishops and other ecclesiastical Authorities, after having made her submissive remarks, she did not oppose the measures that were demanded by others, those same persons having after some time to acknowledge that the measures taken by the Servant of God were just and prudent, and they had to follow them. What I have now set forth, I can affirm from personal experience, it having happened to me, in the many years I was in the direction of the Daughters of St. Anne in the house of Naples, to wish to take measures or to oppose some of the dispositions given by the Servant of God; she never opposed my will though making me note that she did not agree with me. Time then, as I indicated above, proved the Servant of God right»204.

The same Most Eminent Cardinal alludes in his deposition to two very significant aspects where in a particular way the exquisite prudence of Mother Rosa is evidently manifested: her relations with Fr. Tornatore, the choice of persons for the various offices and the measures she promptly took for the government of the Institute:

«Mr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, priest of the Mission, who had had a great part in the foundation of the Institute, habitually lived in the same houses of the Institute, and often followed the Foundress and the other sisters who went about visiting the houses. He with much zeal worked for the right running of religious life, but often too was influenced and impressed by those religious who were either reproved or punished by the Foundress, and often sided with them against the very measures of the Servant of God. As is easy to understand, this dualism was a cause of tribulation for the Servant of God, who with her habitual system, while she did not wish to oppose the said ecclesiastic, in her mind well felt and noted the inconvenience resulting from it in the discipline of the various communities. Here too I can affirm that time gave full satisfaction to the Servant of God.

In the choice of persons destined to the various offices in the communities I absolutely exclude that she could have been guided by secondary ends, notwithstanding that sometimes the person chosen did not meet her expectation [...].

As regards the temporal good of her subjects, she always gave measures that corresponded to the end. I cannot deny that in several houses inconveniences occurred on this point, but I absolutely exclude that this depended on negligence of the Servant of God, and I prove this by the fact that she took energetic measures, when she was informed, and after having verified or had verified the deplored inconveniences, which not infrequently were exaggerated by religious of little spirit»205.

77. — In a very complete overall panorama, finally,

p. 90

Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV at the Roman Process, gives us on Mother Rosa's prudence this fine description:

«The Servant of God possessed prudence not in the human sense but the evangelical. In granting or denying permissions this virtue was revealed. To Sr. A. Maristella Calderone, who on a certain occasion asked her permission for certain penances, she denied it, because of the delicacy of her physique. So I heard and also read in some letter. Whereas to another sister, who asked her a similar permission, she not only granted it, but even urged her to extraordinary penances. Admirable was her prudence in maintaining peace in our houses, and by this virtue many cases that seemed desperate were well settled. So once she put in order by her prudence a magistrate who had harassed our sisters so much, as I myself heard from the Servant of God: ‘With one glance at the Tabernacle — she then told me — I put them all in order’. Her prudence shone in having legally disposed the goods of the Institute in such a way that it could not be despoiled by others' intrigues. So one can see from the suit brought by the Barbiellini family»206.

«While she was so frank that she made known to us sisters all the affairs of the Institute, she nevertheless with much prudence kept silent about things that could have hindered, if they were known, her government. So once, in the presence of a certain superior, she did not wish to say where a sister was, while the others present were mistaken in naming the house.

If by strict duty she had to take some measure of rigor, she took good care not to offend either social proprieties or the honor of the sisters. So when she had to remove some sister from a house, a measure to which outsiders, even powerful, objected, she held to reasons that could offend no one. She was admirable in the devices she used when relatives of sisters importunately asked her that their sister relatives be sent to this or that house nearer to them, or employed in this or that office. She, with patience, with skill, in answering, found a way to convince them of the inopportuneness of their requests. Her prudence shines in having known how to hide for forty years the sufferings and macerations of her body»207.

78. — In her magisterium as Superior General she never failed to guide her religious and above all the superiors of communities in the practice of prudence. In this respect full of wisdom are the directions she gave to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni:

«Truly let such correction be made only to give pleasure to God, and never let the least interior feeling of ours have part in it, but only see that the words that must come from us be edification to the sisters, and serve them as amendment on feeling them in the heart, and make it so that it be reproved to such a degree that it have no other refreshment to restrain its throbbings except to seek anxiously to amend itself; charity; the gentleness of the words of a mother who corrects her daughters makes the heart of the sister unable to do other than correct itself and become a Daughter of St. Anne»208.

«I recommend that you be well on guard, do not trust appearances, because when a person makes these maneuvers you must know that, in their external actions, they seem good and full of zeal, this is to give you a lesson, or rather, allow me so to express myself, you being still a novice in the malice of the world, I need to give you some clarification»209.

2. Justice

79. — That Mother Gattorno complied with that form of Justice proclaimed by Jesus in the Gospel: «Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's and to God the things that are God's»210 remains evidently demonstrated by her perfect observance of the Commandments of God, the precepts of the Church and the rules and constitutions of the Institute, as was illustrated above ad abundantiam.

Since, then, Mother Gattorno always shunned evil and practiced good, preserving her life unblemished until death, we can with good reason catalogue her among those Just of whom Scripture says:

«Happy the one who fears God and has great affection for His commandments»211.

But the Servant of God distinguished herself also by that other form of justice called particular and its potential parts, which is described as constans et perpetua voluntas unicuique ius suum tribuendi212; of her, in fact, it can be said: «Numquam fecit malum et opprobrium adversus eum (proximum) non suscepit».

First among the testimonies we bring on the justice heroically practiced by the Servant of God is this of Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process:

«She never harmed justice. I remember well, from report received, that she was accused and dragged into court by a priest, as if she had violated the contracts made between her and him with due authorizations and relating to a work of charity, for which the Servant of God was invited to lend the assistance of her daughters. The Servant of God, however, emerged from that suit with full triumph both on the civil side and on the part of the ecclesiastical Authority, which at first had given credence to the priest. With her there was no respect of persons and she did not tolerate this defect in her religious [...].

As regards the financial relations of the subordinate houses, the Servant of God arranged that they could provide for themselves, as customary; those houses that had a surplus sent it to the Servant of God, as superior general, for the needs of the generalate house, of the novitiate, and of other houses which the Servant of God judged she ought to assist.

Complaints arose on the part of the sisters on this point, saying that the local superiors deprived their subordinates of necessities in order to make themselves acceptable to the superior general; I know that in a few houses this inconvenience occurred, but I also know with what severity the Foundress reproved those superiors, and this clearly says that the deplored inconvenience cannot be attributed to the Servant of God»213.

The same Most Eminent Cardinal Granito di Belmonte informs us of the profound sense of justice with which the Servant of God knew how to fulfill her duties as mother without thereby neglecting the obligations of a religious:

«Torn from her family, the Servant of God never neglected her duties as mother according to the flesh, and always occupied herself with her children, especially in what concerned morals. One must not believe, however, that she let herself be so absorbed by these cares as to neglect even in the least part her duties toward the Institute founded by her. Having procured a good education for her daughter (who had unfortunately become deaf-mute at a tender age), so as not to be disagreeable even in conversing, she was glad as of a providence of the Lord on learning that a young man of the Roman aristocracy, Count Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei, had taken an interest in her daughter and had asked for her hand in marriage. Even after the marriage the Servant of God continued to occupy herself with her daughter in order to make less painful her unhappiness issuing from nature.

Sometimes she also helped her with money; nor does it seem to me that she can be blamed for this, since it is to be noted that of the money given to her by benefactors, some was presented to her with this specific purpose, of using it for her particular charities. The Servant of God, however, was so delicate that she hesitated to give a small part to her daughter and son-in-law without having asked counsel, and she asked it of me myself several times, and I always judged that this was well-ordered charity, to help that unhappy daughter of hers, who was constrained by violent means by her husband to have recourse to the Servant of God, all the more since I knew that these subsidies were offered to the Servant of God for works foreign to the Institute»214.

80. — To this same sense of justice toward her children Card. Granito di Belmonte again alludes when he testifies about the sufferings her son Alessandro caused her, above all by his estrangement from religion until, finally, he died as a good Christian:

«About thirty years ago one of the sons of the Servant of God, Alessandro, died, who, although attached to his mother, made her suffer much by his private conduct, and the greatest anguish of the Servant of God was to see him far from God, while a grave illness (consumption) brought him day by day closer to the grave. The Servant of God spared nothing for his temporal health, and at the same time worked so that he would return to God, and with this aim too she offered herself with temporal penances to the Lord. She was heard by the Lord, because the son, sent to Naples for a climatic cure, grew worse and reached the point of death. Then he made his confession, noting that he was glad to be able to give this consolation to his mother. The illness having given a little respite, he went to Piacenza, where he died with the last religious comforts»215.

On this aspect of justice practiced in a Christian way by the Servant of God toward her children, Francesco Gattorno, brother of Mother Rosa, witness II at the Genoa Process, offers us precious information:

«Rosa gave her daughter a dowry of about eighty thousand lire, securing it on a property in Sampierdarena, which had come to Rosa by paternal inheritance. Since at the time of this marriage my sister found herself a little short of cash, I paid the expenses of the marriage and also gave what was needed for the wedding trip [...].

Rosa constituted the above-mentioned dowry by securing it on the property, because at the time of the marriage it was not possible to realize conveniently the value of the property, which afterward, by an agreement with the railway, was sold for about one hundred and twenty thousand lire. The operation liquidated, the dowry was invested in a holding at Podenzano, in the district of Piacenza. My sister having thus fulfilled her duties as mother toward her daughter, ought, at least on this score, to have had no troubles; but the matter went quite otherwise.

The daughter, stirred up and pushed by her husband, sought to gain advantages not only from her mother's family goods, but also from what, through the work of the sisters, by donations, was being accumulated in the Institute. My sister, as she had scrupulously given her daughter what could fall to her of the family goods, so she wanted rigorously preserved to the Institute what belonged to it.

She thus had for many years to resist the unjustified insistences of her daughter, who seized every occasion, spied every moment to find herself alone with her mother in order to repeat her requests. I myself in Rome many times attended my sister's small meal, already frail in health, in order to free her by my presence from her daughter's annoyances, at least for the time of her very small repast. My sister never wished to yield on this point»216.

p. 94

81. — Great love for justice, heroically practiced, Mother Rosa also showed in her relations with her son Alessandro. Here too Francesco Gattorno, brother of the Servant of God, furnishes us evident proofs of the sense of justice that always animated Mother Rosa's way of acting before her family:

«No less sorrows she had from her son. He, corresponding little or nothing to the education received and to the family traditions, made a poor success. At first he never found a way to settle down stably; he then went to Buenos Aires, where he stayed about two years. He then returned to Italy, stayed in Florence two or three years, afterward looking after a small paper mill on the Liri; he finally went to Piacenza, where he died, assisted by his mother, shortly after 1890. He, in order to obtain from my sister consent and help to contract marriage, confessed a fault not committed and the consequent paternity of a child. Before death, however, he revealed to his mother that he had deceived her regarding this paternity and that the child was not his at all. So my sister had to suffer painful vexations on the part of her daughter-in-law, who among other things obtained provisional sequestrations and also a search of her mother-in-law's room. She therefore had to defend herself to safeguard the Institute and sustain the suit for the disavowal of the legitimacy of the supposed grandson. I learned from several sisters that in these straits my sister felt very great sorrow. In this suit of disavowal I too intervened as witness, and was able to show with irrefutable documents that for more than two years before the birth of the supposed grandson, Rosa's son had lived uninterruptedly in America, while the woman had always lived in Florence. In this lawsuit too my sister gained full victory, which however did not diminish her sorrows»217.

82. — From love of justice there arose in Mother Rosa her extreme fidelity in the fulfillment of duty, as Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi, witness II, deposes at the Roman Process:

«The Servant of God occupied herself with solicitude about disciplinary observance and for this not only watched over the house where she resided, but also visited the others with zeal. Sometimes she wrote not only to the superiors, but also to simple religious, as she did also to me a couple of times, exhorting, encouraging, comforting. If she noticed some lapse in observance, she made herself heard, yet she was not harsh, although she did not yield [...].

The Servant of God was not only solicitous for the spiritual good of her religious but also took every care that nothing necessary be lacking to them, and wanted the other local superiors also to watch over this point. She was in a special way tender toward the sick, having them cared for as well as she could, and in the conferences she gave us, she greatly recommended the care of sick sisters, and likewise recommended them to the local superiors. When then they grew worse, and I myself noticed it, she was solicitous that they be provided with religious comforts. And such solicitude she required equally of the local superiors for their subjects [...]. The solicitude of the Servant of God for spiritual and temporal things was not limited to her religious, but extended also to all those entrusted to the care of her sisters; to the sick, that they be comforted and provided with the sacraments in case of need, to the girls received for education, for their religious and civil instruction, that nothing necessary be lacking to anyone [...].

I am persuaded that the Servant of God observed the commandments of God and the precepts of the Church with diligence, and was faithful to her duties as daughter, wife, widow, and finally religious. This persuasion I formed from the exemplariness of her life in the time that I knew her, from the exhortations full of conviction that she made to us, for it is good to know that almost every Sunday she convoked all the religious to instruct and exhort them about their religious duties, about the duties of how to behave with the sick, in short in all that she thought opportune for them [...]. I noted the exemplariness of the Servant of God's observance of the rules, she thus giving the example of what she taught us»218.

83. — She was irreproachable in the exercise of the virtue of justice as Sr. A. Maristella Calderone, witness I at the Naples Process, expressly declares:

«The justice of the Servant of God has been for me irreproachable. I have already deposed that she was most exact in her duties toward God, whose laws she faithfully observed, and whose wills she respected with heroic resignation. Toward neighbor she always showed herself just, giving to each what was due. She was always submissive and deferential toward the authorities both ecclesiastical and civil: she was always exact in compensating the services rendered to her, and in giving the due wage to workmen. She was always grateful for benefits received. She was also very careful to respect and have respected the good name of neighbor»219.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, adds:

«As to justice I believe I can say with all certainty that the Servant of God never refused to give to others what she owed. Before dying she came to pay 40 thousand lire for the house of Sampierdarena, and was very glad, because she had set herself to settle that debt before dying. She imposed on the workmen who worked in this house, and had the superiors impose on their workmen, to keep the feast holy. She then worked so that even outside workmen would keep it holy. She never gave offices or posts in the Institute out of partial affection, but only in view of their being suited to the office to which she chose them. The Servant of God was most grateful toward those who benefited the Institute. Of the lady who left the Gargatano estate to our Institute, she kept her portrait on her desk to remember her more often. In memory of that priest, benefactor of our house at Prato, who also gave the money to furnish the guest quarters of this house, she had a large portrait made to be kept on display in the house at Prato.

p. 96

She then recommended to all her sisters that they pray for benefactors, as she left written in the rules, and for deceased benefactors she had Masses celebrated»220.

Sr. A. Michelina Negri, witness X at the Roman Process, who lived beside the Foundress for a full twenty years until her death, offers us this profile of her great love of justice:

«The Servant of God visited her religious houses very often, and one may say she was almost always on the road. To know better the real state of them, she sought to arrive unexpectedly and was most minute in her inquiries. And this solicitude of hers in the visits she had constantly until the last months of her life. For the visits she did not even care for her health, and sometimes, on arriving at the houses, she had to go to bed at once, because she could bear her illness no longer. When then she could not go personally, at the beginning she sent Sr. Benedetta Carrega, and sometimes her first secretary, Sr. Francesca Camisa. Even after the provinces were made she did not dispense herself from visiting the houses of the various provinces, and one may say that she always made the visits herself, not relying on the visits of the provincials [...].

In the distribution of offices she did not let herself be guided by affections of partiality, but chose for them the sisters according to their aptitude and capacity. On this I never heard any reproach made by anyone to the Servant of God. She was also a skilled administrator of money. She did not possess great education, because she was educated in times when not much was usually given to women; but it was said that if she had had occasion to educate herself more, she would have become a prodigy for her multiform talent, because, notwithstanding the little education, she understood accounting well and everything else»221

«From what I know, and from what I have heard said, the Servant of God, in assisting her relatives, never at any time neglected her duties toward the Institute, to such a degree that her relatives even complained, such as her son and son-in-law, who said: ‘After all she must always remember she is a mother’. But the Servant of God to such remarks answered: ‘For my children I have done what I could, I have provided for them and settled them, so let that be enough for them. The first place for me must always be held in my mind by the Institute’»222.

84. — For reasons of justice she recommended generosity toward workmen, as Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, XV witness at the Roman Process, recalls in her testimony:

«The Servant of God possessed the virtue of justice in the most perfect way not only toward God, but also toward men. She never denied workmen the due wage, and rather said to her sisters: ‘If you are short of means, limit yourselves in alms, but as to the workmen be generous’, and I heard it myself. She distributed offices without regard to human respects; she gave corrections with just measure and timeliness. Her recognition and gratitude made her pour out thanks to superiors and benefactors. Her phrase was this: ‘I do not know how to say anything, I do not know how to thank enough, but the Lord will surely think of rewarding you’. She then cared so much that the superiors should scrupulously exercise justice so as to give no handle even to the ill-disposed, whether in hospitals or in boarding schools, and she reminded them of gratitude as a duty. She never ceased to thank the administrators of some hospital; if they had thought they should not charge her the expenses of some sister sent by her for some operation, and had wanted to keep her and treat her as a guest. And her thanks did not cease even for things of much smaller account. She enjoined the sisters that prayers be said for benefactors; and if some sister failed to recite after the meal the three Glory Be for benefactors, she pointed out not only the lapse against the rule, but also that against gratitude»223.

3. Fortitude

85. — This is one of the most evident virtues in the ascetical picture of Mother Rosa Gattorno. Not only as a cardinal virtue but also as a gift of the Holy Spirit. Admiration comes spontaneously as in the Book of Proverbs:

«Mulierem fortem quis inveniet? Procul et de ultimis finibus pretium eius»224.

Naturally, it is not so much Mother Rosa's courage, her intrepidity in certain critical situations, in which she knew how to resist abuses, injustices and divergences of views that leave one admiring, as rather her long-standing capacity to withstand physical pain, to set her hand to the foundation of the Institute and to bring it to completion in a social context so often and in so many ways discouraging.

Indeed, from the whole of her life and from the testimonies of eyewitnesses the twofold side of the exercise of Fortitude is very well outlined: that of «aggredi» and that of «ferre». In both the one and the other field of expression of Fortitude one can discern fairly well how much belonged to her natural disposition and how much, on the other hand, was surely the effect of the gift of the Spirit, cultivated and strengthened by personal effort.

Already in adolescence and during early youth, before marrying, the Servant of God showed herself full of the Christian virtue of fortitude, as her brother Francesco, witness II at the Genoa Process, well recalls, with words reported by us above when we dealt with the virtue of justice (see nos. 79-83). But this fortitude of Mother Rosa already presents outlines of authentic extraordinariness when, married more out of obedience to her parents than from a true matrimonial vocation, she soon began to understand that her marriage would be a real disaster. Here is the deposition of the aforementioned Francesco:

«The marriage was downright a disaster, and the cause to my sister of continual sorrows and sacrifices. The hoped-for happiness went away with the carriage of the wedding trip. We accompanied her for a stretch, that is, as far as Varazze, on the nuptial journey; then, we relatives having returned home, she went on to Nice and Marseille, where the financial failure of her husband awaited her. She at once appealed to Papa, who ran to Marseille to bring in that desperate case what help was still possible, succeeding thus in saving some small thing from that financial shipwreck and then had to bring back to Genoa his daughter with her husband, receiving them in the paternal home.

There the misfortune awaited her of her first daughter being born deaf-mute; the husband around 1855 went to Russia to occupy himself in a trading house set up by his brother-in-law and brother of mine, and from there returned in about 1857 already ruined in health, and in fact died of tubercular pneumonia before 1859. In all these trials I was able to observe, together with her deep sorrow, her inflexible strength of soul. She suffered especially for the deaf-mute little girl who, being ill, could not make her illness understood, expressing herself only with cries and tears»225

86. — When the moment came to put into practice the idea of founding the new Institute and having obtained the approval and blessing of the Archbishop of Genoa and of the Holy Father Pius IX, Mother Rosa had occasion to show that strength of soul and that magnanimity in undertaking great things for the glory of God, which would be to the very end of her life one of her predominant attitudes. We take from the testimony of Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, the following information:

«She set out her plan to the family, and naturally an uproar arose. Her good mother especially felt troubled, because, advanced in age and ailing, she saw herself assisted by her daughter with so much love and sacrifice, even at the cost of whole nights of rest. The Servant of God nevertheless showed herself always tranquil and intrepid. The Servant of God had already gathered for her foundation some Genoese young women, and when the moment of departure came, the good mother, to dissuade her from abandoning her, stretched herself out on the threshold of the door (in the memoirs of the Servant of God I found it written that her mother sat on the threshold) saying: ‘Let us see if you will have the courage to pass over my body’. The Servant of God then (it is always she who told me these things) made a leap, and flying was at the station, where she found the young women summoned by her for the foundation and with them left for Piacenza»226.

The whole history of the foundation, then, from the beginning to the day of Mother Rosa's death, was a continual obstacle race in which the Servant of God, day after day, had a thousand occasions to practice the Christian virtue of fortitude. Many are the witnesses who exalt in the Acts of the process the exquisite fortitude of Mother Rosa throughout the vicissitudes of the foundation. So the Princess of Fitalia, witness XXXI, ex officio, deposes at the Roman Process:

«The Servant of God was the strong woman of the Gospel. She was never overcome either by adversity, or by illnesses, nor discouraged. She herself told me that for her suffering was a delight. At the beginnings of the Institute particularly, as Mother Carrega told me, the poverty was extreme, and the oppositions and adversities also manifold; but nothing prevailed against her strong soul.

Sr. Maria Teresa Sorrentino, when she was in the world, herself thought of becoming foundress of an Institute, at the suggestions of Cardinal Guarino. The Servant of God liked this young woman very much, and wanted her in her Institute, and one day she said to me, regarding Maria Teresa's project of foundation: ‘To found an Institute one needs a breast of bronze’»227.

From the aforementioned Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, we cite further this allusion to the difficulties of the beginning of the foundation:

«In the first beginnings of the Institute she struggled amid a thousand economic difficulties and also because there were those who did not look on the Institute with a good eye; a priest came to say to her: ‘But what are you doing here? Close shop and all of you go home, it is better’. And she answered that despite all difficulties, since it was the work of God, it had to continue, and that Pius IX had told her that it would last until the end of the world.

She did not yield before the overbearing of administrators of works entrusted to her, and when the honor and decorum of the Institute had to be upheld. I recall that at Rossano, I think, the administrators of the hospital wanted to rescind the contract with us, circulating facts not nice for us. The Servant of God put the matter in the hands of a lawyer, and made the administrators keep their place [...]. The Servant of God was always suffering in body, but always resigned; and in this state she found herself from the beginning of the Institute; and not only was she always resigned, but always very active»228.

p. 100

Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, adds:

«The Servant of God in the foundation above all and also in the governance of her Institute naturally had many difficulties to overcome, but from what I have heard said, and from what I know directly, she never gave herself up as beaten, nor ever lost heart, but went on constant and firm in her work»229.

Sr. A. Vittoria Archetti, witness IV at the Roman Process, recalls:

«At the beginning of the foundation bitter war was waged against the Servant of God in Piacenza, especially by Freemasonry, and the more she busied herself in works of charity, the bitterer the war became. She was accused of being a sanctimonious woman, an impostor, a deceiver. Notwithstanding this war the Institute progressed rapidly and is now spread in Italy, in France, in Spain, in Portugal, in Brazil, in Bolivia, in Argentina, in Peru, in Chile, in the United States, in Africa»230.

Mons. Carlo Amirante, witness XIX, ex officio, at the Naples Process, deposes:

«The Servant of God was adorned with Christian fortitude. It is well known with how much courage and firmness of soul she sustained adversities, so that in the holy Church of Jesus Christ her Institute might do a little good. When, over the openings and closings of houses, she met with oppositions, she consoled herself with it as a demonstration of God's will and, having recourse at the foot of her Crucified, held firm to her decision. I recall that once, because I had obstinately opposed her counsel concerning the retention of a superior, she resisted me strongly. And since I persisted obstinately she yielded out of prudence, but I had afterwards to repent of it bitterly and with my humiliation I had to return to her to have her set things right»231.

87. — The secret of her unshakable fortitude she found in the joyful and universal acceptance of the divine will. Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV at the Roman Process, deposes:

«The Servant of God was strong both in joys and in adversities. We sisters always saw her upright and never bowed under the weight of difficulties and the gravest sorrows, although her heart was most sensitive. We noticed it especially in the period of the Apostolic Visitation in which some weaker sister lived in anxieties and palpitations; and she with her calm was our strength.

Sometimes sorrows wrung tears from her, but they did not succeed in taking from her resignation to the divine wills. And when painful news reached her, in which she saw grave losses for the Institute and her maternal heart grieved, she spoke to us of the duty to conform ourselves to the divine will. It seemed incredible how a human creature could have so much command over herself.

p. 101

From the abbot Tosti of Foligno I heard that Freemasonry had singled out our sisters in that city and that one night, the Servant of God being in our house, fire was set to the great door, and that the Servant of God, having heard a noise, looked out, saw the flames and a man with a knife in his hand. Scorning the danger, she went down with her sisters and passed through the flames followed by them. On the occasion of the explosion of the powder magazine in 1895, I think, we were all terrified, and we ran to the Servant of God, who was not calm only for herself, but knew how to infuse it into us too.

She was also scornful of risks on the occasion of epidemic diseases. She had, in short, no measure in giving herself, caring not at all for dangers.

As to natural character, one saw that the Servant of God must have been very sensitive and lively; but she had made herself mistress of it so as not to let herself be overcome by her liveliness in any circumstance, even the most provoking, as I observed many times. Sometimes I saw her indignant, angry never. Her firmness was her most beautiful side, because she seemed an unshakable rock on which she founded the Institute. If she did not see in it the glory of God, requests could well be made to her whether by favor or with insistence; it was useless, she did not budge»232.

Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, witness VIII at the Roman Process, thus highlights the fortitude of the Servant of God:

«She was a truly strong woman, and declared that the day on which she had nothing to suffer seemed to her lost, and she desired to carry the cross. To us sisters she instilled courage with energetic words, besides with her example. Never did she lose heart under the cross, and she used to say: ‘To suffer for me is to enjoy’. The Servant of God was of a lively and ardent character, but one saw very well that she repressed herself from the first years that I knew her. And I noted in this virtue a continual crescendo»233

Cardinal Domenico Serafini, witness VI, ex officio, at the Roman Process and Apostolic Visitor of the Institute, also acknowledges in Mother Rosa the virtue of fortitude:

«It seems to me I heard it said that during Mother Gattorno's life her son-in-law Barbiellini gave her much trouble, seeking to wrest money and promises from her by even violent means, and that Mother Gattorno resisted»234.

Alluding to a severe trial suffered by Mother Rosa in relation to the Most Eminent Card. Verga, Prefect of the Bishops and Regulars and Protector of the Institute, Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, extols Mother Rosa's firmness and fortitude:

«By temperament the Servant of God, as I knew her, was neither lively nor phlegmatic, but calm, of that calm joined to resoluteness and firmness. This firmness was always put to the test through so many difficulties of life, but these were the cause of this virtue of hers shining all the more, being perfected. Her firmness and prudence found itself in a hard trial before a highly placed ecclesiastical person (Card. Verga)»235.

88. — Studying the disposition and temperament of Mother Rosa, Fr. Lázaro Iriarte presents her to us as a woman of strong and courageous soul, full of serenity and balance, enriched by great sincerity and frankness, objectivity and practical sense, a cheerful spirit and a sense of humor and an exquisitely feminine sensibility, affectionate and tender, but free of sentimental subjections:

«In the critical moments of her life — writes Fr. Iriarte — (Mother Rosa) showed herself mistress of herself, resolute and courageous. So, for example, in the family events, as wife and as widow; in the alternative of leaving her own children and parents to consecrate herself to God's interests; in the attitude taken toward persons and situations, some strong and humiliating, that she had to face as foundress.

Ill from the beginning of her widowhood, weakened by fasts, vigils and other penances, subject moreover to the pain of the hidden stigmata and to the ardors of the heart, which produced frequent fainting, she worked tirelessly in her office, undertook long and heavy journeys, visited the houses of the Institute listening to all the sisters, dealt with prelates and benefactors...; and she managed to master her own weakness and tiredness, so as to appear, as the saying goes, always in form.

And she knew how to infuse courage into her collaborators, the superiors, the individual sisters and other persons who confided in her»236.

And the same Fr. Iriarte continues:

«In the catalogue of virtues there is one linked to fortitude, virtue and gift of the Holy Spirit, and it receives the name of magnanimity and also of audacity: it helps to overcome pusillanimity before obstacles to be overcome. In a note to Mons. Granito di Belmonte Mother Rosa wrote: ‘A line in haste, to give you good news: I have made the contract for the schools (in Naples), and they are already at work. Long live audacity! What do you say? It is not audacity, but only confidence in my God’»237. Here is the secret of that energy of character that caused admiration: Mother Rosa was a woman of faith; she was sure that, in her own weaknesses, she could always count on the fortitude of God: I can do all things in him who strengthens me238. And she was convinced she had God on her side, since the Institute founded by her was the Work of the Lord; therefore in her writings the text of Saint Paul leaps out now and then: If God is for us, who can be against us?»239.

89. — Magnanimity and audacity she recommends to the religious Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti, whom she wants «clasped to the unshakable tree of the cross»:

«My little daughter, these are times of tribulation and of crosses: let us try to embrace everything with holy resignation, let us hold tight to the unshakable tree of the cross so as one day to find ourselves saved and blessed for an eternity; courage, resignation, let them be our two shields that sustain us in all the immense trials found in the work of the Lord»240.

To be truly strong in trials Mother Rosa suggests to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni to «grow and be strengthened in the spirit of God»:

«It is time that you become strong women and no more; grow and be strengthened in the spirit of God, for this is the only thing we must want and seek with untiring zeal»241.

She herself confesses to having the experience that suffering and pain, if accepted with Christian fortitude, are transformed into a source of relief and joy. She reminds Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni:

«A single line to tell you that you must make yourself strong; I feel your pains and they all come down upon my soul; I would like to be able to relieve them for you by taking everything upon myself, but, dear little daughter, know that after the suffering and the pain you will see that you will have to console yourself with the very pains you now suffer. Courage, my dear, and you will see that good Jesus will come to console you»242.

The anguishes that torment her are many and tremendous; she therefore asks for prayers so as to be able «to maintain peace and cheerfulness under the weight of so great a cross». She writes to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa:

«My dear, I am in the most tremendous anguishes; pray and have others pray, so that I may always be able to maintain peace and cheerfulness under the weight of so great a cross; I assure you that I am content and that it always seems little to me; but I also know that if He who gives me this taste for suffering withdrew a tiny bit, ah!, I would certainly be the ugliest monster and all in me would be lost. Ah, good Jesus! He, my superior, makes balsamic ether come out of thorns to intoxicate us; sure that you too will ask Him for this, and beloved Jesus will give it to you»243.

4. Temperance

90. — If one rethinks what has been said about her excellent self-mastery, her perfect interior lordship, the total submission of the passions achieved above all in the period of the Servant of God's long religious life, the heroicity of this virtue in Mother Rosa becomes conspicuously evident. Indeed, from her external way of acting the eyewitnesses received the clear sensation of finding themselves before a person who had attained full control of her faculties, her senses, her very biological needs.

To such harmony of her powers Mother Rosa had come, besides by special gift of the Lord, also by continual exercise throughout life, from the years of childhood. In her is found fully applied the exhortation of Saint Paul to the Christians of Corinth to carry imprinted in one's own body the mortification of Jesus, so that his life may be manifested in our body244.

Indeed, in the life of Mother Rosa voluntary mortifications, physical and spiritual, were a very remarkable constant which the Most Rev. Fr. Lázaro Iriarte studies in a profound and exhaustive way in his book «Fisionomia spirituale di Rosa Gattorno»245. We recall in this connection that Mother Rosa Gattorno was a specialist of true devotion to the Cross and to the Passion of the Lord and nourished a most rich spirituality centered on reparative suffering.

To understand better the characteristic attitudes of Mother Gattorno in the constantly heroic exercise of this virtue of temperance and above all the great penances practiced by her, so often more admirable than imitable, these introductory words of the aforementioned Fr. Lázaro Iriarte seem to us very useful:

«Bodily mortification, in one form or another, is a constant of the whole history of Christian asceticism, indeed it is inherent in any spiritual tension also in other religions. The motivations can be various, as various are the interpretations such a phenomenon arouses from the anthropological point of view.
