Certainly, there can be deviations that have nothing to do with the religious relationship with God, such as: the Manichean hatred of one's own body, masochistic satisfaction, fanaticism, the delirium of self-destruction, pharisaical exhibitionism... But the traditional exercise of works of penance has its root in the evangelical metanoia, which is a permanent tension of conversion and, therefore, of asceticism and renunciation, as a condition of following Christ (Mt 16:24), as reparation for one's own sins, renewed struggle against one's own disordered tendencies until mastery of them is obtained246, keeping the spirit free and ready for the call of the Lord.

But, from the theological point of view, there is a deeper justification: to share in the mystery of the suffering Christ, of redemptive pain, offering the Savior as it were a supplement of voluntary suffering, so that he may continue his victimal immolation for the glory of the Father. Many great penitents have made their own the motivation of Saint Paul: ‘I rejoice in the sufferings I endure for you, and I complete, in my flesh, what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ, for the sake of his body which is the Church’247.

All this together constitutes the why of the atrocious and, let us say, exaggerated penances of Rosa Gattorno, who lived in a historical epoch in which the asceticism of fierce assault on one's own body seemed to have been superseded»248.

91. — Undoubtedly, Mother Rosa being endowed with so sensitive and dynamic a nature, she had to struggle hard to acquire that self-mastery which all who knew her inside and outside the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne so admired in her.

The testimonies we continually glean here and there among the witnesses of the Processes are very clear in this regard. Sr. A. Amante La Barbera, witness XXXVIII (8th ex officio) at the Roman Process, deposes:

«In temperance her virtue shone. I heard it said by the usual sisters who lived closer to the Mother that from childhood the Servant of God loved the poor so much and for them deprived herself of food to distribute it to them. Having become a widow, she began her life of continual abstinences. She no longer took either meat or broth. And yet meat and especially salami pleased her greatly, as she expressed herself confidentially with me. And to mortify herself the more she often went to the kitchen on feast days to cut us our portions of salami; she no longer tasted anything sweet, nor fruit. I even saw her so many times remain almost fasting with only the soup, because the dishes were prepared with too much care. To our insistences she answered: ‘No, no, daughters’, and delicately pushed the dishes away. I do not know how that body could keep itself up on so little food. She never ate between meals, I never saw her take anything of food or drink, except some rare times to quench the burning thirst in the great heat of summer; and to resist she rather resorted to immersing her hands in cold water, and so she continued her torment of thirst. She warmly recommended temperance to us, and also told us: ‘When you eat a dish of beans, beware of greed’»249.

Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi, witness II at the Roman Process, adds:

«External mortification she showed in the bearing of her eyes, of her whole person, in food, in rest, and in the other most harsh penances she practiced. When she corrected, I never noticed in that year in which I was here, and never heard others note, that the Servant of God made an uproar in corrections, but she was always calm. Not only did I not hear this said, but on the contrary I heard from other sisters, that is, that she was always calm.

The ordinary food of the Servant of God was potatoes, and these in small quantity. Not totally excluded from her food, however, were milk, eggs, butter and fish. Everything was cooked in oil. Meat was absolutely excluded from her food, and likewise wine, she being content with water only.

I know that she slept little and on a straw mattress, without a mattress, and that in the pillow there was a rather thick chain arranged in a circle, on which she laid her head [...]. Besides the Fridays of which I spoke in another session, on all occasions of tribulations, and whenever she felt need of special graces, she withdrew for whole days into her room, and we religious all believed that at that time she did penances and prayed»250.

92. — Almost all the witnesses highlight the most temperate life the Servant of God led; almost all also point out her great mortification in eating, in drinking, in sleeping. So, for example, Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore:

«Most temperate I always knew the Servant of God. Setting aside this, that she took neither broth nor meat, because they harmed her stomach, she was nevertheless for the rest very frugal. Her ordinary food was potatoes, onions, vegetables and ordinary fish, in general what the secretary or the cook mother provided for her. Sometimes, not knowing what to give her, they fried her an egg, but she did not eat it willingly. When she felt her strength failing, she herself asked sometimes for an egg yolk, and I never noticed that she took two. I vaguely recall that for I do not know what ailment egg yolks did her much good; and then they were given to her. She was induced only in her last illness to make use of milk.

When I entered the Institute I saw that they prepared a small cup of chocolate for her in the morning, but it was very little; but then I saw that in the following years she took only coffee without sugar in the morning and so remained until lunch»251.

On Mother Rosa's temperance in sleeping here is the deposition of Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process:

«She slept very little, the Servant of God. I was able to understand, by speaking with her herself many times, that at night she had not gone to bed, and I was able to understand it and better still from the present Mother General. Seeing in the morning the great work done by the Servant of God during the night, she said to her in amazement: ‘But all this, Mother, when did you do it?’. And she answered simply: ‘When I could’. When she then went to bed I am sure she did not sleep more than two or three and a half hours. Not only I, but the sisters too heard and saw her going about the house, going to the sisters' dormitories, etc.»252.

p. 107

Among her favorite penances abstinence and fasting excelled, as Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV at the Roman Process, informs us:

«The Servant of God knew no intemperance of any kind. In food she was frugal in an unbelievable way. In Holy Week, on Thursday and Friday she ate nothing at all. She shut herself in her room and left it only to attend the services. She fasted on the vigil of the Immaculate Conception and the last days of carnival in a way that moved us to compassion. At indeterminate but frequent times, she returned to fast strictly. On these days Sr. A. Borromea brought her the soup, and she tasted a few spoonfuls, and left the rest; so when she brought her the first dish of vegetables, two forkfuls, and enough; and so with the other dish. She said, to hide her fast, that she felt unwell. She was, however, unconcerned in these fasts, and tried not to let them appear. We observed, sometimes, that of the roll of which half always remained for her, the other half, breaking it, she had made disappear with the cutlery on the plates that were taken back to the kitchen»253.

93. — She was very temperate also in speaking. In this aspect her control and absolute self-mastery were striking. Here is the deposition in this regard of Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process:

«Of a very sensitive character, she moderated herself in her expressions. I never saw her indignant, even in the gravest cases. In these I did see her weep at times, but not become indignant, nor utter a word of complaint against the cause of her pain: at most she said to us: ‘This thing truly was not needed: but God permits it; his will be done’. After this she withdrew to the church or to her room; and if we crowded around to stay about her and comfort her, she said to us: ‘No, daughters, leave me alone’. After a little we saw her tranquil, as if nothing had happened»254.

Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, recalls that Mother Rosa's temperance was also manifested in illnesses:

«There is no need to say in what way she tolerated her infirmities; even then her spirit did not detach itself from mortification; even knowing that from some medicine or food her sufferings would have been eased, she did not resort to it, and, if offered, did not make use of it [...]. The life of the Servant of God as regards food was, in short, a continual and harsh Lent. The quantity of her food was very limited. In the morning a simple black and bitter coffee»255.

With regard to the penances practiced by the Servant of God, Card. Granito di Belmonte prefaces this clarification of his:

«It does not seem to me that one can in any way doubt that the

p. 108

Servant of God sinned by excess in the exercise of her virtues. If I had to observe any excess in the Servant of God, it would be that of her penances, and I myself pointed it out to her at times, telling her to think of her obligation to preserve her health for her Institute. The Servant of God, however, answered that her penances did not prevent her from attending to her duties and discharging them. And the facts have shown that she was quite right since she always attended to and discharged her office perfectly, and ended her days at an advanced age»256.

94. — Most prudent and very discreet in everything, Mother Rosa knew how to keep her great penances in the deepest secrecy, even if the sisters supposed they were many and not common. Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, who assisted Mother Rosa in the last moments of her life, deposes as follows:

«I myself dressed the Servant of God, helped by three other sisters, Sr. Anna Consolata, present provincial of Upper Italy, Sr. A. Rosella, surname I think Bolognini, now deceased, and the then mistress of novices, now likewise deceased, whose name I do not recall. On that occasion we found on the upper part of her chest several rows of scars, which had already healed some time before; so too on the two forearms and the two arms a row of scars of so many little dots. On the left side of the rib cage I found something like a cut, which I saw to be quite deep, but I did not observe it well. It was of a violet color: I washed it like all the rest of the body. Since in this operation I was doing the main part, I tried to hide it from the other sisters who therefore did not see it»257

4. Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, witness I at the Piacenza Process, reveals the following details about the penitential life of the Servant of God:

«She slept in a wretched little room, the dreariest and most uncomfortable of the house, of which she herself always kept the key, never permitting anyone to enter it. From this the community inferred that in that room the Servant of God kept instruments of penance with which she chastised her own body. These suspicions became for us a reality when, she having passed to a better life, it was possible to enter the said room. Having myself the key, which was sent to me from Rome by the new Superior General with the charge of seeing whether in that room there was the Crucifix enclosed in a case, which case was given to the Servant of God by Princess Fitalia, a Crucifix which, according to what the Servant of God herself declared, had addressed some words to her, I was greatly surprised to find the room full of instruments of penance. A large cross formed by two beams, evidently made by the Mother herself, on which cross the Servant of God climbed fastening her wrists with iron devices, another cross stretched on a bench on which she lay, as is presumed, wearing the habit of a Franciscan tertiary, found in the room. On the pillow she used, a thick iron chain is sewn, on which it is inferred she rested her head. She slept on the straw mattress without mattress and without sheets, with a simple blanket. In the same room were also found several scourges, with sharp iron points, hairshirts also made of iron wire with points which from their shape it is understood she put on her arms and her sides, and other instruments such as a crown of thorns, cords with iron points, etc. There were also found in the said room cloths stained with blood; sometimes the Servant of God was seen to appear in community with her face and forehead with little wounds from which blood came»258

5. Sr. A. Apollonia Marchetti, witness VIII at the Naples Process, adds:

«The Servant of God used instruments of penance; I, who had care of the linen, noticed that the Servant of God's shirt bore the imprint of a belt with stains of rust, blood and pus, so that even after the wash, to remove the rust stains perfectly I used salicylic acid. Said stains were observed not only by me, but also by the sisters assigned to the laundry, among whom I recall Sr. A. Virginia Gaggi and Sr. A. Orsola, who at present I do not know in which house of our Institute dwell»259.

95. — United to the redemptive mystery of Christ, Mother Rosa lived the mysticism of suffering with mind and heart fixed on completing the sufferings of Christ according to the saying of the apostle Paul. In this profound and redemptive sense of the mysticism of suffering Fr. Iriarte finds the meaning of the great and in so many respects harrowing penances of the Servant of God:

«Rosa Gattorno belongs to the throng of so many great lovers who, like Saint Teresa of Avila, Saint John of the Cross, Saint Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi, Saint Veronica Giuliani, made of suffering, so to speak, the why of their existence: a mission, that is, to complete the sufferings of Christ (Col 1:24), collaborating in his redemptive immolation. In such a mission suffering is inseparable from love: love is the cause of suffering, suffering is the expression of love. In Mother Rosa's Memoirs one passes constantly from harrowing pages, where she lays bare her sufferings of spirit — darkness, abandonment by God, temptations to despair — to others in which we see her enjoy the intimate loving union with the Beloved, or experience the impetuous fires that oblige her to cry out: ‘Love, you are making me die!’. The same cry of sorrow-love her heart exhales when she experiences the shivers caused by the internal wounds of the hands, the feet and the side or by the chain embedded in the flesh»260.

p. 110

CHAP. VI
HEROICITY OF THE RELIGIOUS VOWS AND OF HUMILITY

96. — The singular spiritual-ascetical edifice of Mother Rosa Gattorno is enriched with further elements if one considers her Poverty, Chastity, Obedience and Humility, whose outstanding exercise in her has already been implicitly alluded to in the preceding pages. These virtues being linked and connected with other principal ones, mention has indeed already been made of them. But, besides being fitting, it is appropriate to make here a specific examination of each of them, because in a certain sense each shows a special relevance in the picture of Mother Rosa's evangelical perfection. It can be affirmed that Poverty, Chastity, Obedience and Humility shone in her even more than the cardinal virtues, and constitute, so to speak, a characteristic of great prominence among the notes of her holiness.

Let us see them one by one.

1. Poverty

97. — We do not wish to let ourselves go in emphatic statements, yet the whole body of the Acts, indeed the whole earthly story of Mother Gattorno, speaks the language of Poverty. Born of a well-to-do family, she soon turned away from love of the goods of the earth and, imitating Jesus, made herself poor and embraced Poverty in the footsteps of the Poverello of Assisi, of whom she was a fervent and passionate imitator. She lived Poverty in the perspective and spirit of the Gospel that proclaims the poor blessed; she felt «pleasure» in the exercise of Poverty, it being understood that this love of hers for this virtue, the first proclaimed by Jesus in his Beatitudes, was never in Mother Rosa mere resignation but true joy at being poor and therefore closer to God and dearer to him. Effective and affective detachment from every earthly aspiration, from every human comfort, the continual aspiring to Heaven and planning everything in function of it, complete the picture of the outstanding Poverty of spirit — and also material — of the Servant of God.

In the process Acts the spirit of poverty of the Servant of God often appears: her preference for the poorest, the environment of poverty in which the new Institute founded by her was born, the total simplicity of Mother Rosa's clothing and personal furnishings. That her detachment from things and material goods was true spirit of evangelical poverty is confirmed by the fact that she was of great generosity toward others, while she herself remained deprived even of necessities.

p. 111

Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, witness VIII at the Roman Process, in her testimony refers to the great poverty of the origins of the Institute founded by Mother Rosa:

«In the first times of the foundation the Institute found itself in economic straits, and the Servant of God, to maintain the sisters, had recourse even to selling precious objects of her family, for which she afterwards gave compensation. Because of the economic straits of the first times there was not much on our table, but still one way or another we managed to satisfy our hunger. Sometimes we had recourse also to cornbread and for supper sometimes only to stewed apples with a little sugar and bread. I remember it well, because I too was there in those times. At noon in those times there was soup and a single dish. The sisters, however, were all content, and it is evident that the Lord wanted this Institute, giving them the spirit necessary to overcome these difficulties. The Lord brought into the Institute in the first times persons of excellent and most distinguished families, showing also by this that he wanted the work and blessed it»261.

Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, witness I at the Piacenza Process, attests:

«As to poverty I can attest that the Servant of God showed herself in all her acts detached from the goods of the earth; she wore patched habits: her bearing was humble, that of a poor religious in everything»262.

And Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, adds:

«The Servant of God was always patched, and she patched her own things in the evening, when she went to her room, although we offered, begging her to let us do it. Sometimes, however, Mother Carrega would secretly take away her old habit, replacing it with a new one; but the Servant of God, though obliged to put on the new one, because the old one had been taken away, said: ‘I am never so well as with my old things’, and asked Carrega for it back, who was obliged to give it back to her.

She had, however, an unpatched habit, which she tried to keep nice for when she went to the Pope, and she called it: ‘the Pope's habit’. When she died, however, we did not find even the Pope's habit decent enough to dress her in, and we had to be content with that one, because there was nothing better. Her underskirts too were of ordinary cloth, and she did not want even these replaced by new ones when they were old. The same may be said of the chemises, the stockings, the jerseys, etc.; and she had, in a word, everything old and patched. She was, however, very clean, and recommended cleanliness to us too. Habitually she wore cloth shoes, but sometimes I saw her in leather shoes. She used laundry soap to wash herself. If she noticed that some sister had used perfumed soap, she reproved her.

Very poor was her room here in Rome: I am not speaking of her secret room at Piacenza already described. Of this one, however, I will say that in the last years one could no longer drag oneself up there except with great difficulty because of the narrowness of the little staircase. But sometimes she dragged herself up there all the same. We then begged her to choose as her bedroom the one in which she worked and received the sisters. In this one there were some ordinary chairs, no armchair, a desk, a kneeler of common wood, a bed with a simple straw mattress without mattress. She did not want the mattress even in the last days of her life. She had two pillows just as in her room at Rome. There was a chest of drawers, a screen, a picture of Our Lady with the Child, a St. Anne and a Crucifix. But in that room she slept little.

The furnishing of her room in Rome was this. Besides the bed, as we have said, there was an ordinary little table, covered with black oilcloth, with the Crucifix on it that is now in the chapel; another little table like the other with a drawer, in which she kept her things. She had no bedside table. There were ordinary chairs, a straw-seated kneeler»263.

98. — Mons. Carlo Amirante, witness XIX (2nd ex officio) at the Naples Process, recalls in his deposition the Servant of God's love for evangelical poverty and defends her from several unjust accusations in this regard:

«As for the virtue of poverty, which was the object of her continual recommendations, I observed that the Servant of God kept great cleanliness in her clothing, but often I saw her veil and her habit patched; using ordinary and cheap handkerchiefs; nothing refined in her study, except the image of the Crucifix, always beautiful; never accepting a gift, so that the immense offerings made to her on the twenty-fifth anniversary of her religious clothing were immediately distributed to the various houses.

At this point I note that it was often said among some sisters that those superiors were dear to the Servant of God who gathered and economized the most, even to the detriment of the sisters, sending everything to the generalate house to gain merit with the Mother. This, as far as I know, is perfectly false and I prove it by the conduct of the Servant of God. At the opening of the house of Morigerati, when Baron Pellegrini, of happy memory, and the late Mariano Belli handed over the little income assigned to that house, the Servant of God did not even touch the securities, which were handed over to the late Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega. When it was thought of buying a new house in via Capodichino, here in Naples, the Servant of God opposed it, giving as her reason the grave sacrifices to which the sisters would be subjected. I add that all the money that was sent to the generalate house in Rome, as surplus from the other houses, was destined for nothing else, as the said Sr. A. Benedetta reported to me, than to meet the needs of other poor houses and the movement of the sisters. There was also murmuring about this movement of the sisters, as useless and often they said harmful. But I must in conscience affirm that these continual movements took place for the preservation of the sisters' virtues, as the Servant of God several times confided to me, loving rather the reputation of the Institute than material well-being»264.

The Servant of God, most loving of poverty in the style of St. Francis of Assisi, in whose school she had been spiritually formed, not only lived poverty personally but also sought that the same poverty be evident and clear even in the external appearance of her houses. Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, deposes in this regard: «The somewhat decorous furnishing of our guest house cost six thousand lire, if I remember rightly, and was a gift of a former Dominican, a certain Fr. Benedetto, very rich. He had already shown himself very generous also for our house at Prato, and the superior had turned to him at the suggestion of Mons. Franchi, then vicar general and later bishop of Livorno. The Servant of God complained of this guest house of ours, it seeming to her too luxurious, but she had had nothing to do with it, because it was the benefactor who dealt directly with the purchase. As to the material part of the entrance, that is, marble stairs etc., I remember that when the Servant of God was invited to come and see the works, which were already well advanced, the Servant of God, when she was in the first parlor, let her veil fall, and putting her hands on her hips, turning to her brother Francesco, in a tone of reproach said to him: ‘But what have you done to me, Checco? It looks like a hotel to me!’. And he answered in her ear: ‘Let it be; they will no longer call you a ragamuffin’. Truly at that time we were called ragamuffins. I was present at this episode»265. The example of poverty that the sisters saw in the Foundress was followed by them as good daughters, as Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, witness III at the Roman Process, recalls: «This I can declare, that she (Mother Rosa) held poverty very dear and exhorted us all to exercise it. I remember that in a conference she even disapproved of the use of white handkerchiefs, so that all then used colored handkerchiefs to blow our noses. Seeing the virtue of poverty so exactly exercised by the Servant of God, we other sisters too abstained from things which would otherwise have been lawful, such as the use of fingerless gloves, of the fan, at least in her presence, etc.»266 99. — So great was her esteem for poverty that she liked to recommend it in season and out of season to her religious, for example on the occasion of new foundations of houses. Thus, in fact, Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV at the Roman Process, deposes: «The Servant of God, when a new house was proposed to her, informed herself first of all of how her daughters would be able to fulfill their duties of piety. And she did not worry much about the economic arrangement made for the sisters for the new house by those who invited them. I myself heard her repeat: ‘In the foundations of new houses it does not matter that we find ourselves in economic straits, we shall better observe the rule and the vow of holy poverty. Have trust; work much for love of Jesus, pray much, and you will never lack anything’ [...]. While she recommended poverty so much and did not worry about accepting new houses with restricted means, she nevertheless helped her daughters when they found themselves in real need. The Servant of God always recommended poverty so much and kept watch on this point, not sparing the superiors remarks when she saw that they had provided themselves with something that seemed to her luxury. I myself saw letters on this subject, and in them I saw, for example, remarks about a luxury carpet. ‘A good sign — she used to say — when we are in want in every way; when all goes well on every side, I do not like it so much’. The Servant of God watched that the sisters should not lack necessities. How many times she sent fabrics and other things, writing to the superiors: ‘You will reimburse me when you can, now I know you are not in a position because you have other obligations’»267.

From the beginning of the foundation it was the express will of the Servant of God that the Daughters of St. Anne assist the sick in their homes and practice charity without any previously agreed economic compensation. So recalls among several other witnesses Sr. A. Michelina Negri, witness X at the Roman Process:

«It is to be noted that in the houses where our sisters are to assist the sick at home they had to abandon themselves to Providence for their needs, being unable to demand or ask anything for their assistance to the sick, and therefore they could sometimes be in need, and they received help from the Mother. I said that the houses where our sisters were destined only to the service of the sick at home had no special resources, and this enters into the main purpose of our Institute, since the Servant of God founded it with the purpose principally of assisting the sick gratuitously at home and in the hospitals. When the Servant of God demanded the savings of the various houses, she pointed out that they must be truly from the superfluous, and woe to those superiors who dared to send savings beyond [their means], skimping too much even on necessities in their communities»268.

100. — In the practice of personal and community poverty Mother Rosa recommends taking the example of what happened at Bethlehem, where Jesus came to be born in extreme poverty. So she writes in this regard to Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti:

«Courage, for your tribulations are few compared with the cave of Bethlehem: there was no bed, but only straw, and yet the Son of God chose it for his first dwelling and wished to be born there. The Queen of heaven and earth seated where? On the straw, and near a manger, feeding only on the beautiful light of Jesus. She found everything, the comforts, the delights of the world in that dear little child, he enclosed everything. And you, who can gaze upon him within your heart, behold, you will find every delight if you keep your gaze on him alone»269.

Poverty having been lived in the following of the poor Christ, Mother Rosa teaches her daughters that this poverty must be for them a source of joy and perfect gladness. She writes in this regard to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa:

«Regarding poverty, you tell me you are ashamed; this language I do not understand: ought we to be ashamed of that of which we make a vow? And with God's help we must try to put it into practice. Who was poorer than Jesus? And if we are to be his imitators, we must always be in stables, in caves. You others are neither in caves nor even in stables. If they tell you how poor you are (you will answer): ‘Lord, this is our treasure [...]; so the vow we make imposes it on us, but believe that we are quite content’»270.

2. Chastity

101. — It is gathered from the Second Vatican Council:

«Chastity embraced for the sake of the kingdom of Heaven (Mt 19:12) and therefore for supernatural motives, must be esteemed as an outstanding gift of grace. It indeed frees the human heart in a special way271, so as to inflame it ever more with charity toward all men and, consequently, constitutes a particular sign of heavenly goods, as well as a most effective means for being able to dedicate oneself generously to the divine service and to the works of the apostolate»272.

These words, which summarize the conciliar decree on religious life, seem constructed on the model of perfection put into act by the Servant of God, above all from the moment in which, her husband having died, she remained a widow and the possibility opened to her of consecrating her whole self to the service of God and neighbor in religious life.

The external appearance of Mother Rosa inspired purity, chastity. So expresses herself in her process deposition Sr. A. Maristella Calderone, witness I at the Naples Process:

«From the whole of the life of the Servant of God there breathed a great modesty and reserve, a certain sign of the purity of her soul. In manner she was chaste, in words measured and sober, and it is a fact that never, as far as I know, did she allude to her life before the foundation, when she was wife and mother. Her conduct was for all of us of great edification. In the conferences she gave us she was accustomed at times to allude with much delicacy and ease to the guarding of the senses, which must be chastised to keep them in servitude, and there shone through her words the care she took to mortify herself especially in food, to keep her senses in check»273.

Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, witness VIII at the Roman Process, adds:

«The Servant of God was chastity in person. One had only to look at her to have the impression of her purity. This already says enough about her bearing, as to the eyes and in all the rest. I never heard that she spoke of her marriage [...]. Since we had to be in hospitals and exposed to so many dangers, the Servant of God herself told us: ‘We must keep a very reserved demeanor and never remain alone’»274.

102. — On her demeanor which stimulated others to purity, Sr. A. Vittoria Archetti, witness IV at the Roman Process, expresses herself thus:

«Her most reserved demeanor breathed great love of purity; and in her talks she recommended to us much reserve and demeanor, especially with men. As a consequence of this love of purity she did not want us to distract ourselves in frivolous reading, and this she recommended also to us superiors, that we might watch over it»275.

On the same subject Mons. Pietro Piacenza, witness VII (2nd ex officio), deposes at the Roman Process:

«The demeanor of the Servant of God and her modesty of the eyes were such as to make one immediately notice her great love of this beautiful virtue. And from some incident I noticed how much she loved this virtue, and she wanted her sisters to abstain from any familiarity, even the most innocent, with ecclesiastics, and from conversing with them without necessity»276.

Very significant along the same line is also the testimony given by Sr. A. Cungonda Pacini, witness VI at the Naples Process:

«The Servant of God, as far as I know personally, loved the virtue of chastity very much, since she strove with her talks and counsels to arouse such love in us sisters. For the rest, I can affirm that her conduct was always reserved in every respect, above all when she had to approach persons of the other sex by reason of office: she did so with such dignity and reserve that I, who was sometimes present in the guest house, was filled with great admiration. Her conversations were always inspired by holy things, never vain and idle, and in her whole attitude one clearly saw the virtuous woman»277.

p. 117

Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, witness III at the Roman Process, offers us this beautiful page on Mother Rosa's singular love of chastity and its heroic exercise:

«She was most jealous of the virtue of chastity. She did not want to be touched in any way and for this reason never wished to be examined by doctors, to whom she hardly allowed them to feel her pulse. I do not know whether two days before, and I do not know whether even the Servant of God at that moment understood, the doctor was finally able to palpate her. Such was the ruin of the body of the Servant of God that the doctor declared she had been a corpse already two days before dying [...].

Most modest in her eyes and at the same time at ease. How rigorous she was on this point, and rightly, can be seen from the following fact. A sister was recalled from America because in the hospital she had entered into a relationship with I do not know whom. When she arrived before the Mother, she threw herself on her knees, but the Mother gave her a severe look and went on (the meeting had taken place in a corridor). Then the poor religious, commending herself, called her: ‘Mother, mother’, but the Mother paid no heed and did not turn. I myself was witness of that scene, heartbreaking for me but which shows the fortitude and love of the beautiful virtue of the Servant of God.

In connection with this virtue I have already told of the incident that happened in the hospital of Sampierdarena. The Servant of God having prescribed in the constitutions to report to the superior if they saw a sister a little light-minded on the occasion of assisting the sick, so as to give room to the tongues of the malicious, I asked the Servant of God to be dispensed from such obligation, but she did not wish to dispense me from the said obligation»278.

103. — Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, completes very well the picture of Mother Rosa's heroic chastity:

«Concerning chastity, I will say first of all that the Servant of God did not allow herself to be touched by anyone, not even by the doctor, to whom she allowed only in the last times to feel her pulse. How many times I offered to put her shoes on for her, her feet being so swollen, and she did not allow me. In the last years, however, no longer being able to bend, she was then obliged to have this service done by the nurse. After I had been in the hospitals, however, she let me take her pulse. She never let herself be seen undressed by us, and when we saw her suffering, we begged her to call us at least when she had lain down, and she did so.

I never heard that she spoke of her marriage, and I never heard her speak of her husband or even pronounce his name. With seculars she always presented herself accompanied, and if anyone had come asking to speak only with the Mother: ‘Oh, this is impossible’, she would answer. And this precaution of the rule of always being two together, how she recommended it to us too! If she came to know that some superior permitted herself to appear alone with seculars, one may say she saw red and gave herself no peace. She tried to find out, and as long as she could, she went herself in person to find out and to put the superior in her place.

I remember a certain superior who, to justify herself, in sometimes receiving seculars alone, adduced the too restricted number of sisters she had with her, so that while the others attended to urgent duties, she by necessity had to receive alone seculars whom she could not, given certain circumstances, have sent away. ‘Well then — the Servant of God answered her —, if these reasons are true, I will sacrifice myself to send you one more sister’, and so she did. And this precaution not only with lay seculars did she use and want used also by the sisters, but also with priests.

I remember that in the conferences to the novitiate, explaining how the vow of chastity must be kept, among other things she told us not to gesticulate so much, not to touch one another, and she did not permit this even in jest, nor that they take one another by the arm even for a moment, nor give each other the hand. She, moreover, gave the example with her very dignified bearing and without gesticulations»279.

104. — The following deposition too of Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, brings out well Mother Rosa's love of the virtue of chastity and her great commitment to forming her disciples well on the understanding and scope of this basic requirement of consecrated life:

«With her brothers the Servant of God never took too much familiarity, nor with her son-in-law; and when she went to the parlor for any person who had to speak to her, she always went accompanied. I never noticed in her the slightest act of curiosity when traveling. She did not allow newspapers of any kind to enter the houses of the Institute. I heard from the Servant of God herself that she urged the teachers to be attentive to the girls' books; and she herself wanted to see the books of the postulants when they entered [...].

In the circulars she sent every year, she always recommended that the sisters not give familiarity to the girls, that the nursing sisters keep reserved with other male and female nurses and with the other male staff of the hospital, and in general that no sister ever give her hand to a man. These same recommendations she renewed when she saw the superiors. ‘And when you notice a light-minded sister — she told them —, try to correct her, and if then she does not listen to you, notify me’. She almost never spoke with me of her marriage, except that time when I asked her whether at the celebration of her wedding she had worn the dress with a train. And another time she told me that her little daughter's muteness was due to her having taken a husband. ‘It is a punishment that has come upon me, because I took a husband’. The Servant of God felt as a humiliation the fact of having been united in marriage, so much so that I once said to her: ‘Why, Mother, are you ashamed of having taken a husband? It is not a sin; the Church permits it’. And she answered me: ‘What do you want? I feel a certain repugnance’. For this reason she never spoke of it, not even with the other sisters. When the Servant of God came to know that a sister was a little light-minded, she placed her under a capable superior, and first made her do the spiritual exercises, and was accustomed to say: ‘Then they mature with the years and improve’. She could not bring herself to send them away from the Institute, and I do not recall that she sent any away [...], because — she used to say —, if they are not for the Institute, St. Anne will see to sending them home. I do not mean by this that she did not dismiss novices, when she did not see them suited to the Institute»280.

Card. Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, defines Mother Rosa as «a jealous guardian of the virtue of chastity»:

«She was a jealous guardian of the virtue of chastity. When she heard of deeds contrary to this virtue, from her mouth came words such as well showed all her inner and profound horror. It need not be said, therefore, how much she inculcated it in her religious, how solicitous she was in removing from her communities everything that could even remotely offend it; and the promptness she had, when she noticed something contrary, in taking energetic measures, and if necessary, even expelling from the Institute whoever it might be»281.

In forming her religious to the practice of chastity she did not forget the necessary asceticism and the use of the means traditionally recommended by masters of the spirit. Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi, witness II at the Roman Process, reminds us of this:

«She was most jealous of the virtue of chastity. Not only in our rules did she insert some precautions for guarding this beautiful virtue, but also by word of mouth she effectively exhorted us to use all the means necessary to preserve it intact. These means and precautions were: never to separate from one another when attending the sick, never to give the hand to persons of the other sex, never to be alone in the parlor, flight from idleness, prayer, etc. She then recommended to the superiors that if they saw anyone a little light-minded they should tell her at once. Often she repeated these things to us by word of mouth»282.

«She tried to raise the more timid sisters, upon whom it made an impression to assist at operations which our rules permitted, to a supernatural reason, so that they might look at everything in Jesus and for love of him»283.

3. Obedience

105. — Obedience was certainly not an easy virtue for Mother Rosa Gattorno. Her strong and tendentially authoritarian character was not really made for obeying without difficulty, but rather for commanding.

p. 120

And for this reason the merit of Obedience was greater, in whose exercise she trained herself from the years of childhood with great and evident personal efforts, to the point that she even accepted to marry in order the better to obey the will of her parents.

According to the depositions of the witnesses, who we recall were all eyewitnesses through long-standing, direct and thorough knowledge of the Servant of God, it results that obedience ended by becoming so connatural in Mother Rosa's religious being that she arrived, as the Second Vatican Council says, at

«submitting in a spirit of faith to superiors, representatives of God, placing herself under their guidance at the service of all the brothers in Christ, as Christ himself did»

284. Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV at the Roman Process, deposes:

«Her respect for authority, and in the first place for the Pope, was profound, moving. And she did not fail not only to exhort the sisters, but also seculars, when they came, to ask an audience of the Holy Father, public or private, so that they might have occasion to see him from close by, and thus dispel from their minds all the ill reports against the Pope. ‘Let us bring — she said — as many people as we can to see the Pope’.

I saw the Servant of God show herself radiant with happiness, because to the question: ‘Who was the Pope’, a little dark-skinned girl of seven had answered: ‘He is the Vicar of Jesus Christ’. That time when after the General Chapter she led her hundred and eighty superiors to Pope Leo XIII, it seemed that she with her Institute offered her heart, her unconditional devotion [...].

Her devotion and obedience she rendered not only to the Holy Father, but also to his representatives, that is, to his College of Cardinals, and first of all to the Cardinal Protector. She made known to the sisters the fine qualities and characteristics and the merits of the Cardinal Protectors toward the Institute, even of those whom we had not had the good fortune to know personally.

I remember the recommendations she made to the sisters that they should revere with great honor their Cardinal, if they had the good fortune of having him as Pastor of the diocese in which they were, and to these Cardinals resident in the diocese she took care to bring the homage not only of those few sisters who were in that diocese, but of the whole Institute. I saw various letters on this. And she was so delicate toward them that once, as I recall, she noticed that there was not much space between the date and the signature of a letter to a Cardinal, and observed that in that lack of etiquette there was a lack of regard for the high dignity of the Cardinal»285.

Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, recalls:

«Her veneration for the Supreme Pontiff was always profound, and her sentiments were revealed in her speaking with me and with her religious. This veneration which she had for the Supreme Pontiff was manifested also in that which she had toward his representatives, who shared in the authority of God. Full of respect and veneration she was likewise toward whoever bore the priestly character. Particular then was her veneration for her confessors and also for her directors although from these she did not always receive satisfactory answers to her questions, as regards communications made to her by the Lord because of which her spirit remained in anguish; the Servant of God, however, received these anguishes as a trial from the Lord, and the sentiment of veneration for him who directed her did not weaken in her in the least»286.

106. — Of this veneration and submission of Mother Rosa toward the Hierarchy Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi, witness II at the Roman Process, also speaks to us, recalling how «deferential and respectful toward the Apostolic Visitor» of the Institute the Servant of God was:

«She had great reverence and veneration for the Supreme Pontiff, the Bishops and any ecclesiastical Authority, as was revealed by the way in which she inculcated in us too reverence and submission to the Church.

She was deferential and respectful toward the Apostolic Visitor, and at that time, having come to visit me while I was in via Garibaldi, she told me that she wished to resign from her office of Superior General, but that her daughters did not permit it [...]. The Servant of God prayed for the Pope and inculcated in her daughters likewise that they should pray, and we have a special daily prayer prescribed by her. She prayed and made us pray for the whole Church. She wanted likewise that prayer be made in a special way for the Clergy [...]. She exhorted us all to deference and obedience toward confessors»287.

We find the root of Mother Rosa's obedience in her distant family life, as Sr. A. Apollonia Marchetti, witness VIII, declares at the Naples Process:

«The Servant of God, as her mother, Signora Adelaide, reported to me, was always docile and obedient, indeed the said lady called the Servant of God, her daughter, a pearl. She was most obedient to ecclesiastical superiors, whose dispositions she always carried out. Sometimes when some disposition of the local bishop did not seem just to us sisters, the Servant of God wanted it to be obeyed without discussion, and said that superiors must always be obeyed, that if they err they are the ones responsible. She held the person of the Roman Pontiff in great veneration and I, who accompanied her sometimes, saw with what devotion and respect she presented herself at the audience of the Holy Father, respect which she instilled in all of us, and docility and respect toward all was a characteristic note of the Servant of God»288.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, transmits to us this fleeting but interesting memory on Mother Rosa's obedience in the family, before the foundation:

«The Servant of God was always most obedient and never failed in the least in this vow, when she was a religious. Her mother loved her dearly, precisely because she was so obedient, as I heard from her brothers, who loved her so much when she was little, because she was good and obedient to whoever commanded her. And she was moreover attentive to everyone from childhood. If at home she saw that something was needed she at once lent a hand, without anyone asking her»289.

107. — She married also out of obedience, but willingly and freely, as Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, has deposed in her process testimony:

«Rarely did she speak to me of her affairs, and when some word had escaped her mouth that could put her in a good light, she showed herself alarmed, and immediately added: ‘But you will not tell it to anyone, will you?’. And so she cut short her talk. She also told me that after making her first Communion she always felt the vocation to religious life, but that she could not speak of it in the family, where she would have met decided resistance, especially from her father. She therefore continued, as best she could, secretly and with the complicity of good Manin (a domestic), her holy works, until, a cousin of hers, a certain Custo, having asked her father for her hand, he obliged her to marriage, and I believe he obliged her because she said to me, speaking to me about it: ‘I did nothing but obedience’. But — she added further — for this my not having followed the vocation I felt in my heart, I had at once deserved punishment from the Lord, since the daughter I had at once was deaf-mute’. So saying she wept»290.

The motto of Mother Rosa's obedience was these words which she repeated so many times: «This must be done, because it has been ordered to me»291. The same Sr. A. Camilla Valentini recalls:

«The Servant of God was most obedient to all her superiors. As for the confessor, we argue that she was most obedient to him too, because if sometimes we said to him that for charity he should have the Servant of God take this or that, we saw afterwards that she took it, whereas before she resisted our insistences. She herself called us, her Assistants, to counsel, and we could freely express our opinions, of which she took account. She first let us speak, and then set forth her opinion, asking us what we said of it, and so it happened that sometimes we yielded, sometimes she yielded.

She recommended obedience to us much, and to the superiors she said that if they wished to obtain obedience from their subjects, they must give the example of this virtue first themselves. She was accustomed to say, as I heard her several times, that she found no greater happiness than being faithful to her rule and to the common schedule»292.

Sr. A. Maristella Calderone, witness I at the Naples Process, among the memories she keeps of the Mother Foundress, does not forget her example of perfect obedience:

«I knew the Servant of God when she was advanced in age and Superior General of the Institute founded by her. I too had from her an example of dependence and obedience, since in the individual houses she wanted the local superior to remain in her own place when she went there to stay or to visit, and to exercise equally the functions of superior notwithstanding her presence. To us then she always recommended obedience to superiors, to confessors, and above all to the Bishops of the places where our houses were»293

We conclude with this beautiful deposition of Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV at the Roman Process:

«She presented to us the virtue of obedience in such a way as to make us absolutely fall in love with that vow. ‘As air is indispensable to you for living — she told us —, so obedience is for religious life’. ‘A religious without obedience is like a shadow that walks about the cloister without belonging to it’. Once for St. Anne, after giving a thought to others, she gave one also to me, saying to me: ‘You will have to go to paradise through the virtue of obedience. Until now you have scraped along with this virtue; but you will have to exercise it in a perfect way with its qualities; for obedience must be blind, prompt and slave’. And my pretending to be terrified at this last word, she explained to me how such slavery is that which gives the widest freedom. ‘You will understand better later — she added — and you will be able to tell me’.

She instructed the superiors on the way of giving obedience. She wanted them to conform themselves to characters, and not to use very grave words, such as: ‘Under precept of obedience’ for very light things, ‘because — she said —, confusion would thus be generated in timid and scrupulous souls, between the substance of obedience and the form.

She then was so deferential in conversation toward what others said, toward customs, counsels, that nothing more could be desired»294.

108. — Not without a sincere feeling of admiration Card. Granito di Belmonte gives this judgment of his on Mother Rosa's obedience:

«In the lines of conduct that God directly traced for her in her interior communications, the Servant of God stopped when the authority of superiors or spiritual directors showed itself contrary. In these cases the Servant of God felt the duty, especially when it concerned affairs of the Institute, to set forth candidly and with submission her observations, leaving, however, the will of the superior free. Her obedience extended also to small things»295.

Sr. Fabiana Orsi confesses that the Foundress, where obedience was concerned, was clearly maximalist and demanding:

«Strictly observant of the smallest rules of her Institute she demanded the most exact observance of them from all of us [...] and admitted no word of discussion, as I myself heard, when she exhorted to the exercise of this virtue of obedience»296.

Obedient herself to the rule of the Institute without compromises, she had become a fine prototype of regular obedience for all the Daughters of St. Anne. So she is presented by Sr. Fabiana Orsi herself:

«I confirm having heard it said that all her daughters, in the 33 years in which she lived the life of the community, admired her as a living model of the rule, since they could not catch her transgressing even a smallest part, or departing in any act from the common method of living»297.

Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, recalls:

«She had herself photographed always only out of obedience. On the occasion of the first departure of our sisters for America, these adapting themselves badly to going so far without her photograph, it was then imposed on her for the first time out of obedience to have herself photographed. Of this obedience I heard speak not only from sisters, but also from herself, who said: ‘Oh, that time they imposed on me that I pose!’. This distressed her so much, especially because it seemed to her she had given bad example to her sisters. The second photograph was imposed on her by Cardinal Verga, at the request of the sisters; and it was taken in two poses, one seated, and the other standing. And since the Servant of God adapted herself badly, the Cardinal himself resigned himself to posing too for the first time, so as to induce the Servant of God more easily»298.

4. Humility

109. — Since Mother Rosa Gattorno had, as we have seen, a high conception of the majesty and holiness of God, she inevitably had to nurture a low conception of herself. From the whole of the impressions of the eyewitnesses and from her behavior it is clearly deduced that it was Humility that drew upon her the gazes of predilection of the Lord.

p. 125

Due proportions observed, one may well apply to Mother Rosa the expression of Mary of Nazareth, never recalled enough:

«The Lord has looked upon the Humility of his handmaid [...] and has done great things»299.

From how the witnesses expressed themselves and from the things they reported it is very well seen that Mother Rosa's humility sprang from the heart, and was profound and true, and manifested itself in so many spontaneous and convincing forms. It is fitting to leave the word to the witnesses.

Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV at the Roman Process, presents the humility of the Servant of God as the virtue that most characterized her:

«If the Servant of God was great in the exercise of the other virtues, she excelled above all in the practice of humility. She wished that her person disappear as much as possible. On the occasion of the exhibition of sacred arts at Turin, she, to a sister who asked how to behave before the Royals who would attend, answered: ‘You ask me these things? I really know nothing: I have never dealt with the great’. In this connection it comes to my mind that once she had to present herself to the duchess of Genoa and was obliged to have recourse to friends to give her suitable clothes, she being without them. This fact I have heard told many times by our sisters and also three or four months ago by one of our superiors from America, come here for the Chapter, who had known personally the mother of the Servant of God and a sister.

The conduct of the Servant of God was humble not only before dignitaries, but also with the sisters, with whom she was ready to yield in differences of views. Looking at Jesus Christ in the poor, it seemed she wished to make herself small and disappear before them. I saw in a sister who was so ill as to cause nausea, and the Servant of God performed the lowest services for her. Once, I, coming from outside and having found her in bed, made as if to kiss her feet, but she refused and began a discourse on humility, protesting that she was nothing and did not wish to be anything.

Many priests were surprised to see that the Servant of God went to the secretariat to give them the first greeting. Of her great humility I heard speak in a special way from a priest of Borgo S. Donnino. I heard Mons. Gaetano Pomarici say: ‘If the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne has developed rapidly, we priests can well say that it is owing to the great humility of the Foundress’. And from many other persons, both by word of mouth and in writing, I heard the humility of our Mother Foundress extolled. Among these I recall a senator, a prefect, a bailiff.

Not only on my part can I affirm that the Servant of God persevered in the exercise of the theological and cardinal virtues, of our vows and of humility, on which I have deposed, having never perceived in her any blemish of fault or of any imperfection, but I can also say in all conscience that from year to year I saw her always progress in the love of God, in detachment from creatures and in the other virtues enumerated above»300.

110. — Sr. A. Michelina Negri, witness X at the Roman Process, adds new clarifications on Mother Rosa's humility:

«She did not want to be called ever General, nor Foundress. ‘The Institute was not founded by me — she said —, but by St. Anne. I have been only an instrument in the hands of God. You think me who knows what, but it is because you do not know me well enough’. She never spoke of her own affairs and still less did she exalt herself. And if in anyone her ability shone forth, she tried to cover it, and give the credit to another. For example, if for the foundation of some house she sent either Sr. Benedetta Carrega or Sr. Vincenza, her first secretary, and praises came to her for the well-succeeded foundation, she turned them back upon her envoys, reserving nothing for herself.

She did not allow even us to kiss her hands. Going to visit Cardinals, she announced herself only by the name of Sr. Rosa Gattorno, as Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega told me, and she sat in the anteroom, not in evidence, and so many who had come after passed ahead of her, and she waited in patience [...]. I recall that once the Servant of God had to point out to the superiors gathered together for the spiritual exercises the defects she had noted on her round of their houses; after having set them forth with very mild words and with much sweetness, she knelt before them asking pardon if she had exceeded in speaking. The superiors were greatly moved by that act, left the meeting room with tears in their eyes, so that when we asked those sisters what had happened, they told us what I have said.

At Piacenza I myself saw her so many times wash the dishes, and help in other chores in the kitchen. I also saw her sweep other rooms besides her own. And when she did these services, quite content she said to us: ‘These things, you see, I know how to do very well, these suit me, while you think me who knows what’. In this house I heard it told that a novice of this same house was surprised one day by the Servant of God while sweeping the corridor of this guest house; she took the broom from her hands, saying to her: ‘Let me do it, for I am cold, and so I warm myself a little’, and she went on sweeping»301.

Mother Rosa's humility is striking when, in all sincerity, she believes herself an authentic sinner and feels unworthy to be Superior General of the Institute. Sr. A. Amante La Barbera, witness XXXVIII (8th ex officio) at the Roman Process, recalls:

«Most humble was our Mother; she declared herself the greatest sinner, the worst of all, capable of nothing, and that her Crucifix was the one who carried the house and the Institute forward. And when she said these expressions, one saw the intimate persuasion, and that she profoundly felt their truth according to her. If a sister put on the address of letters ‘Mother General’, she sent the address back. Once she did so also with me, writing to me together with it: ‘Never dare again to call me Mother General’. She was fearful of having to render account to God for her Institute. ‘It would be good — she said — if they put another in my place for the good of the Institute, but when I am obliged to come, I cannot abandon it’. ‘Without humility, without charity, without observance of the holy rules — she told us —, one does not enter Paradise’. As she taught us, in the care of the sick she lent herself to the most menial services.

When one conversed with her, she enjoyed our thoughts, although by talent and by culture she could have kept us all in our place. She knew French, knew how to play the piano, sang with a fine voice, embroidered finely, and yet she told us that she did not know how to say anything, that she did not know how to do anything. She never spoke of herself»302.

111. — From Princess Fitalia, witness XXXI (4th ex officio) at the Roman Process, is this expressive deposition:

«She called herself ‘donkey, nefarious sinner’ and similar expressions, and with such an accent that one could not in the least doubt her persuasion, and one had to think that she had such lights on divine holiness as to oblige her intellect to reveal them to her with horror. By surprise I sometimes managed to kiss her hand, for otherwise she would not have permitted it. If I learned anything from her that might make me grow in esteem for her, she did not tell me out of self-love, but only to do good to my soul, and moreover only with brief and fleeting hints»303.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, points out particularly in Mother Rosa's humility her desire to be despised:

«She loved to be despised, asked it of the Lord, and found herself content in humiliations and in contempt. She said, sometimes, in my presence, addressing the Lord: ‘My Jesus, what do you leave me here on earth to do? I do nothing but sin; I am good for nothing but to offend you’. She wished to appear ignorant, and to hear her, she knew nothing. If sometimes she made a mistake in speaking, or something was badly done by her, she was ready to point it out before the other sisters, saying: these are my virtues; I am good for nothing, I am really a beast who understands nothing, and other similar expressions. She never pointed out anything good, she herself never spoke of it, and did not want to hear it spoken of by others»304.

Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, repeats the same things on the virtue of Mother Rosa's humility and also brings a fine episode that occurred in this regard between Mother Rosa and the Blessed Card. Dusmet, Archbishop of Catania:

«The Servant of God had a low sense of herself. When she spoke of herself, she always said that she was a poor ragamuffin, a donkey, and when she wished to say something very noble of herself she said that she was a poor slave of her Crucifix, and these expressions she said with an accent of true conviction, she did not admit praise with regard to herself, and all this is known to me. If her Institute was praised, she referred everything to the Lord, and if she felt any complacency, it was all on account of her Crucifix. She remained very annoyed if some sister, writing to her, put in the address: ‘Mother General’, she grieved more then if she was called ‘Foundress’, and that sister had to be warned; and when she told us of the secretariat to warn those sisters, she added: ‘Your Mother yes, but as for the title of General, let us leave it to those who have merit’ [...].

Once the Servant of God, as I heard from her herself, found a booklet of memoirs about her and the Institute, written by her first secretary, Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, took it and burned it. Once, visiting the houses of Sicily, Mother Carrega and I accompanied the Servant of God to Cardinal Dusmet, Archbishop of Catania. She entered alone to the Cardinal, with whom she remained in a very long conversation, and coming out she showed herself indifferent with us. She only said to us after a while: ‘We must withdraw from that house’. She then settled all her affairs, and withdrew the sisters. Of that conversation we knew nothing, except this, reported to us afterward by Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi, Provincial of Sicily, now deceased, to whom Cardinal Dusmet, speaking of that conversation, said: ‘I remained edified by the humility and submission of your Mother, for however much I told her, and I told her many things, she took it all in holy peace’»305.

112. — Beautiful though very brief and concise is the testimony of Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process:

«As to humility, the Servant of God never liked praise, and if she heard any, she immediately crossed her forehead, as I saw so many times. Woe if she had heard praises of herself from us! Without fail she scolded us and said to us: ‘If you see anything good in me, it is not I, but God who has done it. I am only a grain of mustard seed thrown on arid ground’. If she heard some sister say: ‘I did this, I did that’, she would interrupt saying: ‘Oh, this blessed I!’. And once I heard her say to a sister: ‘You will say rather, I, my donkey!’. I never heard that she praised in any way or exalted her works or those of the Institute. I heard her say so many times: ‘I am a poor wretch; I am a donkey, and if God did not assist me, poor work of his!’. And these words she said when she saw the Institute exalted or praised. She also said that she did not like them to exalt the Institute, because then she trembled. ‘I desire rather that the Institute be opposed and tried, because then I am ever more confirmed that the work is of God’. One saw that when she was despised, instead of being troubled, she rather rejoiced in it, and said: ‘I deserve this and more’»306.

Sr. A. Maristella Calderone, witness I at the Naples Process, hands down to us this memory on the Mother's humility:

«An exemplary humility stood out in the life of the Servant of God. She never asked for nor tolerated preferences among us with regard to herself, uniting herself perfectly to the life of a simple religious. Often she wanted to serve at table us her subordinates and sometimes she also went to the kitchen descending to the humblest acts. Never have I perceived, nor heard from others, that she had haughtiness in command, but always affable, charitable and courteous manners. She treated all equally with grace and sweetness, even humble and common persons»307.

With a spirit of service and of true humility Mother Rosa also did the most menial services in the community, as Sr. A. Apollonia Marchetti, witness VIII at the Naples Process, recalls in her testimony:

«From the whole tenor of her life I can depose that the Servant of God considered herself the servant and the last of all, so humble was she. She lowered herself, though superior, to the most menial services of the community; and I saw her sweep the floor, prepare food in the kitchen, make bread and other things. She thought so lowly of herself that one day she said: ‘After my death throw this body of mine away like a rotten dog’, an expression that made too great an impression on us sisters and moved us to tears»308.

Card. Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, thus alludes to Mother Rosa's humility:

«Of the humility of the Servant of God it suffices to recall what I declared regarding her love of concealment. If anyone pointed out to her that by her special qualities she could do this or that, the Servant of God felt quite confused and declared that she was good for nothing, fit only for the most menial offices. When she knew that honors were being prepared for her by her religious and by the administrations by which they had been called, she felt the need, in her humility, to avoid them»309.

Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, witness VIII at the Roman Process, attests:

«She was distinguished by humility. She did not like good works to be publicized, but wished the Institute to grow in humility and hiddenness. Of herself I never heard that she spoke and even when something turned out well for her, she attributed everything to God not only in her interior, but also in the talks she had with us. And in her humble speech one saw no ostentation, but sincerity and naturalness. When she saw some fine result in the Institute, she said to us: ‘Oh, how good the Lord is to us310!»

p. 130

CHAP. VII
PECULIAR CHARISMS AND THEIR BEARING ON THE HEROIC EXERCISE OF THE VIRTUES OF THE SERVANT OF GOD

113. — From of old the Catholic Church, not without a divine assistance of the Holy Spirit, has held that the extraordinary phenomena recorded in the lives of some Servants of God are not constitutive of holiness. And we know that, in the practice of this our Congregation for the Causes of Saints, the judgment of canonizability prescinds from that on the nature of the extraordinary phenomena. Nevertheless, always according to practice, some inquiry into the consistency and kind of such phenomena is not neglected, in order to establish their attributability, direct or indirect, to the action of God and the contribution they can make to a fuller knowledge of the personality and, above all, of the holiness of the protagonists. It is in this context and with this purpose that in this chapter the extraordinary phenomena in the life of Mother Rosa Gattorno are treated.

1. The gifts and extraordinary phenomena of the Servant of God

114. — Fr. Iriarte writes:

«We come to the theme that most attracts attention in the life of the great mystics and that, at the same time, raises the greatest difficulties from the scientific point of view; indeed, in our case, it is precisely the one that has put a question mark over the psychic normality of Rosa Gattorno. In general, prejudice against bodily mystical phenomena comes from their spectacular character, that is, from the suspicion that, at bottom, there is nothing else than the unconscious wish for exhibitionism. Hence non-believing or simply positivist scientists record all these phenomena — visions, raptures, stigmatizations, diabolical vexations — under certain common denominators of the field of psychiatry: hysteria, hallucinations, erotic sublimations [...]. It must be said, however, that, in the case of Rosa Gattorno, every motive of exhibitionism is precisely to be excluded. Her great concern, throughout her life, was to see to it that no one noticed what there might be of the extraordinary in God's gifts, as also of her bodily macerations»311.

The contemporaries of the Servant of God were unaware of the extraordinary richness of the mystical gifts and phenomena in which, by divine will, Mother Rosa found herself immersed. Had she herself not written her Memoirs and some confidential letters to the priest Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, future cardinal, the secret of these gifts would have remained buried forever with the mortal remains of the Servant of God.

115. — The second Theological Expert, censor of Mother Rosa's writings, Most Rev. Fr. Serafino Ignudi, Conventual Franciscan, lists these mystical gifts of Mother Rosa drawing them from the writings of the Servant of God herself and above all from her Memoirs, in this order:

— «Stigmata in manibus, pedibus et super cor; —

costas elatas super cor; —

scrutationes cordium et visionem rerum absentium; —

crebrerrimas visiones Christi Domini, B. M. Virginis, S. Ioseph, S. Michaëlis Arc., Angeli sui Custodis, S. Annae, S. Francisci Ass.; —

fere continuo visiones animarum in extremo agone constitutarum; —

frequentissimas quoque visiones daemonum, plerumque sub specie belluarum et monstrorum; —

donum curationum; —

cum non poterat frui directione Patris spiritualis, potens et quodam modo sensibilis divinus ductor moderabatur illam; —

poenitentiae admodum extraordinariae: ieiunia, cilicia, catenae, flagellationes usque ad sanguinem cum innumeris percussionibus sibi illatis; —

tentationes omnis generis, numquam contra castitatem»312.

Most Rev. Fr. Lazaro Iriarte groups all these gifts in three series of charisms: two of spiritual-interior order, and one (the third) of exterior-physical order.

Among the phenomena of spiritual-interior order the following are numbered:

— light of discernment;

— penetration of the interior of persons;

— interior voice;

— company of friendly souls;

— signs and foreknowledge of future events.

Among the extraordinary phenomena of physical-bodily order are numbered:

— raptures and ecstasies;

— stigmata and crowning with thorns;

— ardors in the heart and exchange of hearts.

The author also recalls, in the life of Mother Gattorno, diabolical action, to which he devotes, in his study, a particular section, entitled: The part of the devil.

It is not necessary to repeat what, with the language and competence of authentic masters, Most Rev. Fr. Paolino Zavarella, «perito in re medica» (cf. Summ., Doc. G, 3, pp. 863-897), and Most Rev. Fr. Lázaro Iriarte, Consultor of this our Congregation for the Causes of Saints (cf. Summ., Doc. H, 2, pp. 938-1061), have already set forth on the state of normality of the Servant of God, on her spirituality and on her mystical life. It will therefore suffice to affirm now, as a summary of what these illustrious scholars have said and written, that in the personality of Mother Rosa Gattorno, as presented by the informative sources, the writings and the documents, there is revealed a perfect harmony of human and supernatural elements, which made of her a privileged creature on the plane of nature and on that of grace.

2. Sincerity and humility of the Servant of God before the charisms

116. — With regard to the extraordinary mystical phenomena with which she was abundantly enriched by the Lord, whether or not of supernatural character, beyond doubt, says Fr. Iriarte, is

«the sincerity, absolutely irreproachable, with which the Servant of God commits to paper the moment she lived, just as she perceived it»313.

Beyond doubt also is that in Mother Rosa, both for the interior and for the exterior phenomena, the concern to keep them hidden prevailed, so that no one should notice her mystical experiences. So, for example, Mother Rosa herself expresses herself in her Memoirs:

«My Good, when I am alone, do with me what you will: burn me, consume me, annihilate me, but let no one notice»314.

Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, declares in his long deposition Mother Rosa's wish to keep secret the extraordinary phenomena that happened to her and the way in which he came to know of them:

«Though she did not confess to me, (Mother Rosa) opened herself to me about the affairs of the Institute and also about things concerning her spirit. From that time I was always in relation with the Servant of God, by word or by letter. Though knowing the great virtues of the Servant of God and facts which I had to consider prodigious, my admiration never went as far as enthusiasm, both because of my natural character, and also because the Servant of God, in communicating to me some of her interior things, almost enjoined me not to manifest them to anyone, it being her lively desire to be heard in the prayer she made constantly to the Lord, to be humbled, to remain in obscurity and to be despised. And she added that, given the said lively desire of hers, she herself could not explain how she revealed to me the things she was telling me. Both, as I said before, because of my character not easily given to enthusiasm, and because of the said lively desire of the Servant of God, I kept myself very reserved, and so I did not come to know many things I could have known by questioning. The Servant of God showed me such trust as to reveal to me exceptional facts, which I believe I alone know, and she herself sometimes added: ‘This I tell to you alone’»315.

In confirmation of this Mother Rosa wrote on 21 May 1876 in her Memoirs:

«I overcame myself to manifest a certain thing which, out of shame, I had resolved not to say. Oh, how much it costs me to say what my Good does to me! Oh, a thousand times I would say in public the horrid sins I committed, but the graces he grants me, oh, for me it is the most painful pain I can have»316.

117. — From the testimony of Card. Granito di Belmonte, we take further these words which clarify much Mother Rosa's yearning for secrecy and how, providentially, she chose the Most Eminent Cardinal, then still a simple priest, as her confidant:

«The Servant of God wrote — she told me —, by order of God (and by me then well encouraged to continue in these writings) everything that happened in her spirit, whether of revelations, anguishes or trials, and from time to time she gave me a reading of them, and handed me some booklet to read, but with a most earnest prayer not to communicate them to anyone. Showing me these writings was then for the justification of some permissions that she asked of me, I coming through the reading of these to know what had preceded, and so I could govern myself»317.

Evidently Mother Rosa, with discretion and supernatural prudence, sought concealment and therefore carefully shunned the manifestation of the phenomena and mysteries of her interior world even to her own religious. It should not therefore cause wonder that in the Processes the witnesses' statements on the mystical phenomena of the Servant of God are very scarce, or almost nonexistent: evident proof that they were unknown while Mother Rosa was alive and began to be known only after her death.

With all truth one can therefore conclude with Fr. Iriarte that the Servant of God Mother Rosa Gattorno,
