CHAP. VIII
PECULIAR CIRCUMSTANCES AND EPISODES IN THE LIFE OF THE SERVANT OF GOD

123. — A story as complex as that of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno could not be exempt from contradictions and difficulties: her being a mother of a family and at the same time foundress of a religious congregation brought criticism from some persons during her life. But an attentive and objective examination of the circumstances lived by the Servant of God and a serene evaluation of her conduct, far from obscuring her figure, rather bring into relief her heroic virtue, her balance, her constant search for the will of God, her fortitude united with charity.

From an overall examination it appears that the problems raised arise, at bottom, from one alone: the relationship of the Servant of God with her son-in-law Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei and his family: it was Barbiellini's claims and insistences that provoked the complaints of some sisters about the administration and these, in turn, provoked the Apostolic Visitation. To this cluster of problems must be added, moreover, the personal resentment of some sister, which could easily arise from feelings of jealousy and pride.

1. Complaints about the administration

124. — The Servant of God until the end of her life occupied herself with love both with her children and with the Institute founded by her; nevertheless, she was the target, on the part of some, of complaints concerning the treatment of the sisters in some communities: it was said that the Servant of God demanded more than was due, showing a preference for the superiors who sent more money.

p. 139

These accusations are amply contradicted by the testimonies of the sisters and of other personalities heard in the various Processes.

Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, who was superior, Provincial in Bolivia, general assistant during the government of the Servant of God, deposes:

«The Servant of God, as to the treatment of her sisters, wanted it to be that of the generalate house, and this was her invariable order to all the Superiors; and this she wrote also in the Circulars. She did not permit that any sister should lack anything. If any had need, by medical prescription, of special food, she wanted it to be supplied to her. If to some house the means were lacking, she said to the superior: ‘Where you do not reach, I reach, but I want the sisters to be well treated’. When she visited the houses, and noticed that some superior was a little stingy, and that therefore something was lacking to the sisters, she admonished her, gave her counsels, and made her understand that when the sister is well treated she is more content, works willingly and better»329.

125. — It must be borne in mind that the administration of the Institute was centralized and every six months the superiors had to send to the generalate seat the account and the cash surplus, after having retained the sum needed for the needs of their own house. With the contributions thus gathered from the communities, the Servant of God provided for the maintenance of the houses that did not have sufficient income, for the houses of formation, for the infirmaries for sick sisters, as also for other sudden needs: works in the houses owned, foundation of new houses, departure of missionaries, etc.

The sum to be sent to the generalate house depended, therefore, on the different situations of the individual houses and on the administration of each superior. Princess Emilia di Fitalia, witness XXXI at the Roman Process, observes in this regard:

«The Servant of God was so full of charity toward others that I cannot even remotely think that from the local superiors she would ever have accepted for the generalate house anything beyond the superfluous. I noticed in many superiors a great impulse of love toward the Servant of God, so that it may be that they made and had their subjects make some sacrifice to send something more to the generalate house»330.

The same witness also speaks of the treatment of the sisters:

«From what I heard, and from the way in which she treated her sisters, one saw that the Servant of God occupied herself and was much concerned about the good treatment of her daughters, and for this she had even fixed the menus for feast days, so that they might be well treated and at table too there might be a little feast.

I heard it told that the Servant of God herself went down very often to the kitchen to assure herself with her own eyes how her sisters were treated at table, and I heard it said that in the first times she went to do the cooking.

It need not be said, then, how much care she took of her sick sisters. These were her passion, and sometimes she even helped them miraculously. She went personally to the infirmary, tended them herself with charity without limits»331.

126. — Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, brings out the Servant of God's justice in what she asked of the houses:

«What was left over to the various houses (the Servant of God) required to come to the generalate house; and therefore in the visits, when she found useless expenses in the accounts, then she gave warning. I never heard that some superior, to make herself look good with the Servant of God, thinned the treatment of the sisters, and so send a greater surplus to the generalate house. I know that sometimes some superior permitted herself to send something to poor relatives, or to give particular alms without permission of the Servant of God; but she, as soon as she came to know of it, admonished the superior. I myself heard her say to a superior who had done so: ‘Oh! my daughter, if you had told me, I would have given you the money for your relatives’. For, in fact, she was accustomed to help the poor relatives of the sisters.

She did not require from a house more than it could reasonably give. There were those she, on the contrary, had to help. To me myself she said one day, when in the last year I was superior at the Fornaci: ‘What do you want to give me, you who do not have enough for yourself?’; and once, having made some saving, I wanted to bring it myself to the Mother; but she did not even want to receive it, and said to me: ‘Where did you steal them? It is not possible that you could have saved them!’. And it was truly so, since that saving had not come from the ordinary resources, but from some gift and little works done and alms.

To some superior, however, who sent a surplus indeed, but not all that she could have sent, the Mother gave the opportune warning. In short, she required the superfluous and did not want and did not permit that the sisters should lack anything»332.

The interest and concern of the Servant of God for the health of the sisters are recalled by Mons. Pietro Tosti, witness XVI at the Roman Process:

«I myself ascertained how much care and how much promptness she had for the health of her sisters. As soon as she came to know that some of those of Foligno did not feel well, by letter or telegram she called her to Rome, having her accompanied also, if her not good state of health required it. And here in Rome then she provided according to the cases, without regard to expense. I recall having heard her say once, to the superior of Foligno, to whom she was speaking of the health of a sister: ‘If you do not have the means, I will see to it’»333.

Sr. A. Margherita D'Arcangelo, witness XVIII at the Rogatory Process of Naples, adds in this regard:

«The Servant of God had a particular concern for sick religious and I, having been ill in Ferrara, recall that she sent a special religious to assist and tend me and, writing to me or speaking to me when I was superior, she inculcated in me charity toward the sisters and several times told me not to mind the economy in tending the religious and keeping them content»334.

127. — The Servant of God was most loving of poverty and watched attentively that this vow be exactly observed in the communities. She did not fail to call attention and correct with charity and also with energy, when she saw failings on this point, but this did not at all mean attachment to money. Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, who until the death of the Servant of God was assigned to the general secretariat and was general assistant, recalls it:

«I have heard it said, unfortunately, by people outside the Institute whom I could not identify, that the Servant of God preferred those superiors who sent more money to the generalate house, and that she exalted these, notwithstanding that the sisters of these superiors suffered; but these certainly did not know our affairs, and since I, who was for so long beside the Servant of God, never noticed anything that could constitute the slightest basis for this charge.

That the Mother preferred those superiors who more observed the spirit of poverty is true; that she preferred those who consequently ran their houses better is also true; but that directly or indirectly the Servant of God opposed the local superiors who sent less money and obliged them to send more, even with the suffering of their subjects, this is not true.

The fact, however, is that those who better observed the vow of poverty had, as I said, more money to send to the Servant of God, while their houses went better also temporally and without suffering on the part of the subjects (as we see still verified in our houses), and these superiors the Servant of God preferred, not certainly because they sent more money.

I have heard it said that such an accusation was made by the Apostolic Visitor, now Cardinal Serafini. He, when he went to the houses, listened to all the sisters: no wonder that among these some discontented ones were found, but again I exclude that the Servant of God governed herself with that spirit and performed deeds that could give grounds for these accusations»335.

p. 142

128. — The Servant of God was careful to inculcate in the superiors just and loving treatment of the sisters through teaching and above all by her example. Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, deposes in this regard:

«I heard it said by elderly sisters, I no longer recall which, that before I entered the Institute, the Servant of God, visiting the houses, found discontent, I do not know precisely arising from what; then the Servant of God gathered all the local superiors in our house at Piacenza and the bishop himself Mons. Scalabrini gave the exercises. During these exercises the Servant of God treated the sisters with an interest and an amiability altogether extraordinary. When the exercises were finished, having these superiors with her, she said to them: ‘Now then we are agreed. As you have been treated here, so you must treat your sisters’»336.

Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, notes that the inconveniences occurring here and there in the houses can in no way be attributed to the Servant of God:

«As regards the temporal good of the subjects, she always gave provisions that corresponded to the end. I cannot deny that in several houses inconveniences occurred on this point, but I absolutely exclude that this depended on negligence of the Servant of God, and I prove this by the fact that she took energetic measures when she was informed, and after having verified or had verified the deplored inconveniences, which not seldom were exaggerated by religious of little spirit»337.

Relevant, finally, is the judgment of the Apostolic Visitor, Card. Domenico Serafini, witness VI (1st ex officio) at the Roman Process:

«Asked to whom the deficiency of necessities for the sisters themselves in some house was imputed, I answer that, being a true consequence of the general system, they did not impute it to this one or that one. Here in Rome they were in need of money, and so it happened that some superiors made the sisters suffer, while others, however, thought above all of their sisters, who must not lack necessities, and did not let them lack anything. The simple sisters, however, imputed it to the proximate cause which practically and really was the true cause, that is, to the local superior»338.

129. — From what has been set forth it appears that the Servant of God cared with supreme charity for all her sisters, both in the spiritual and in the temporal part. She exhorted her daughters to the observance of the vow of poverty and demanded it: this could be confused with inadequate treatment by sisters of little spirit. Inconveniences did occur, it is true, through excessive zeal of some superiors, or through the illusion of being more pleasing to the superior general, but this can in no way be charged to the Servant of God, as the Apostolic Visitor himself acknowledges.

2. Relationship with her son-in-law Barbiellini and his family

130. — The marriage of her daughter Carlotta was for the Servant of God a source of continual sufferings and a training ground for the heroic exercise of the virtues, above all fortitude, and was also the cause of the sisters' complaints about the administration and of the Apostolic Visitation itself.

Count Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei married Carlotta Custo in 1876. At the beginning he made an excellent impression: he was pious, frequented the Sacraments assiduously, served Mass in the sisters' chapel, was submissive and deferential to his mother-in-law, as Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, attests:

«Count Barbiellini showed himself very Catholic and practicing; and I recall that even during the time in which he waged with us, after the death of our Mother, an unjust lawsuit, he did not omit to receive Communion every Sunday. To church he always brought the children, at home he never omitted the rosary any day. Toward his mother-in-law he showed himself respectful in the first years»339.

The Servant of God, trusting in his honesty, appointed him her general procurator and made use of him for many affairs of the Institute. Soon, however, Gaspare revealed an unsuspected greed for money, so as to make one think he had contracted marriage for pure interest, to enrich himself. After some years he did not even have reserve in veiling his intentions, provoking the indignation of Federico Gattorno, brother of the Servant of God, who wrote in a letter:

«What hurts me most is the publicity of all the family interests so badly denounced that they make one blush, but he (Gaspare) has too much tola to take notice of it. Shame. For the rest, my dear, the whole family is of the same blood and there is nothing to be surprised at. I remember that the countess Felicetta said that Gaspare had the right to do everything since he had made the sacrifice of marrying a deaf-mute. I shall never forget it; and who obliged him?»340.

The Servant of God had secured for her daughter a dowry of 80,000 lire!341 which had been invested in an estate at Podenzano, in the Piacenza area: this money came to the Servant of God from the sale of a house in Sampierdarena inherited from her father; a sum had also been assigned to her son Alessandro. Having fulfilled her obligation of justice, the Servant of God had no other goods to dispose of for her children, except some alms she received expressly for this; the rest belonged to the Institute. Gaspare Barbiellini, for his part, possessed nothing, except the noble title. Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, witness VIII at the Roman Process, recalls:

«I know for certain that Barbiellini had nothing of his own, and that the Servant of God's brothers even had his wedding clothes made for him, as I heard from the mouth of Mr. Checco himself, brother of the Servant of God»342

Francesco Gattorno, witness II at the Rogatory Process of Genoa, brother of the Servant of God, recalls precisely the situation that arose between the Servant of God and the Barbiellini family:

«My sister having fulfilled her duties as mother toward her daughter, should have, at least in this respect, had no trouble; but the matter went quite otherwise. The daughter, egged on and pushed by her husband, sought to gain advantages not only from her mother's family goods, but also from what, through the work of the sisters and by gifts, was being accumulated in the Institute. My sister, as she had scrupulously given her daughter what could belong to her of the family goods, so she wanted rigorously preserved for the Institute what belonged to it. She had thus for many years to resist the unjustified insistences of the daughter, who seized every occasion, watched every moment to find herself alone with her mother to repeat her requests [...]. My sister never wished to yield on this point; I know, however, that the daughter obtained something from Mother Carrega — who, however, gave from her own personal goods — and perhaps from others, who tried by these means to appease the daughter for the good of the mother. But in vain, since the daughter, and perhaps more the son-in-law, with all their maneuvers during my sister's life, tried to gather the elements to bring suit against the Institute afterwards, after Rosa's death»343.

131. — The Servant of God entrusted for some time the administration of the vast estate of Gargatano, near Piacenza, to her son-in-law Barbiellini344. Soon contrasts arose, because of his dishonesty, as Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, witness III at the Roman Process, recalls:

«The Servant of God, being unable herself to go or to send her sisters to preside over the works that the estate of Gargatano, donated to the sisters by the counts Caracciolo of Piacenza, might need, gave this charge to her son-in-law Barbiellini for a while. I do not know what happened, but one sees well that the Servant of God was not satisfied with him, because I heard him himself say: ‘But let the counts look, let them see the books, let them verify them, etc.’. The fact is that the Servant of God took away from him also that office»345.

The rectitude of the Servant of God in giving money to her daughter is brought out by Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process:

«Sometimes she helped (her daughter) also with money; nor does it seem to me she can be blamed for this, since it is to be noted that of the money that was given her by benefactors, sometimes it was presented to her with this determined purpose, of using it for her particular charities. The Servant of God, however, was so delicate that she hesitated to give a small part to her daughter and her son-in-law without having asked counsel, and she asked it of me myself several times, and I always believed that this was well-ordered charity, to help that unhappy daughter of hers, who was constrained by violent means by her husband to have recourse to the Servant of God, all the more as it was known to me that these helps were offered to the Servant of God for works foreign to the Institute. In this regard I recall that sometimes the little grandchildren went to the Servant of God telling that their father mistreated their mother, who then, in her turn, came to report to the Servant of God the purpose of that mistreatment, which was always money»346.

132. — Lawyer Giancarlo Bonfiglio, witness IV at the Rogatory Process of Genoa, who was the lawyer of the Institute already during the life of the Servant of God, speaks of her sense of justice:

«I can assure that the greatest concern of the Servant of God was to defend the patrimony of the Institute from the snares which some of her relatives set in motion; and to distinguish rigorously her own patrimony, which was to serve her children, from the patrimony of the Institute; and this was a frequent theme of counsels she asked of me. I can add this which I know: that benefactors, precisely to rid her of these doubts, in handing her sums, took care to indicate the use to which they destined them, that is, partly for the Institute, and some small part for her family. I recall an occasion on which the marchioness Carrega, in religion Sr. Anna Benedetta, made a gift to the daughter of the Servant of God, she had to complain to me, saying to me: ‘She thinks to please me and instead I suffer from it347’»!

Another jurist, notary Tommaso Monti, witness XI at the Roman Process, chancellor emeritus of the Vicariate of Rome, confirms the justice and prudence of the Servant of God:

«In the act of settlement with her brother Federico, and in any other act drawn up by me, I always noticed in her a sense of justice, and that she did not let herself be overcome by fraternal and maternal love or by anything else to the detriment of the Institute. When the Servant of God thought of making her holographic will, I had some talks alone with her, and on that occasion she told me that everything she could give of her own to her daughter she had given, and that it seemed to her she had placed her well financially, that she believed she could no longer claim anything from her, and that everything she then possessed was property of the Institute»348.

The Servant of God, as soon as she could do so with due prudence, revoked her son-in-law Barbiellini's general power of attorney349, but Barbiellini always continued in his attitude of claims toward the Servant of God and, after her death, toward the Institute, against which he brought several lawsuits, all lost by him. In 1901 an order of the Court of Piacenza declared, concerning him, that he deserved «no credence because he was an exploiter of his mother-in-law and of the monastic house founded by her»350.

133. — Throughout her life the Servant of God maintained her attitude of scrupulous, heroic justice and fortitude, as appears from what she wrote in a letter to her daughter Carlotta:

«You always cry poverty. Oh truly I do not know what to say. Patience! You certainly will not believe it: I have received only 200 lire, and you will do the accounts and see whether I sent them to you or not. What am I to do if I do not have any? and to touch a penny of the Institute I would let myself even be killed, but I will not do it; my soul matters to me»351.

The justice of the Servant of God is also brought into evidence by the Apostolic Visitor of the Institute, Card. Domenico Serafini, witness VI (1st ex officio) at the Roman Process:

«I am convinced that Mother Gattorno disposed justly and rightly, before dying, the economic part of the Institute and of her family. And in fact after her death no compromising documents came to my knowledge for Mother Gattorno herself. Only of importance I was shown a little scrap of paper on which was written a cession of fifty thousand lire in favor of her daughter's family; but while the signature was certainly Mother Gattorno's, the rest of the writing was in another hand. Which fact, together with the signature on the paper, could give rise to the suspicion of some fraud»352.

134. — The proofs that attest the rectitude, justice and charity of the Servant of God toward the Barbiellini family in relation to the Institute are abundant and many, for brevity, have been omitted. From the documents — among which the declaration of Lawyer Bonfiglio353 is particularly important — and from the testimonies, it appears beyond a shadow of doubt that the Servant of God gave her daughter all that was due to her and kept the administration of the Institute rigorously separate from the family patrimony; she further protected the Institute from her son-in-law's greedy claims, after her death, by legal acts354 and by divesting herself of ownership of the Institute's goods, which at her death did not turn out to be registered in her name.

3. The question of Fr. Tornatore

135. — The question of Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, C. M., is raised by Fr. Alfonso Baratelli, witness XXVIII (3rd ex officio), at the Rogatory Process of Piacenza, who states:

«I do not nurture too much veneration for Mother Rosa Gattorno for what I am about to say [...]. In my judgment Rosa Gattorno had no charity with Fr. Tornatore, indeed I add that she showed herself ungrateful toward him, from whom nevertheless the Institute had so many and so many benefits. I have also heard that he was driven out of the Institute through a feeling of jealousy. He, by his virtues, had very great ascendancy over the Daughters of St. Anne, which was not looked on with favor by Gattorno»355.

Fr. Baratelli clearly refers to Fr. Tornatore's removal from the Institute, which took place during the General Chapter of 1888.

Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore had been a valid and precious collaborator of the Servant of God at the beginnings of the Work: the foundress had recognized that it was God's will to change the name of the Institute as he suggested to her: Daughters of St. Anne instead of «Daughters of Mary Immaculate»356; moreover, she had been inspired to have him write the rules357: in them she had seen fully expressed the charism she had received from the Lord, therefore when these were condemned and Tornatore removed from the Institute, she worked tirelessly to have him reinstated and it was he himself, afterwards, who wrote the rule that was approved. Tornatore did not limit himself to spiritual help to the foundress: he took care of the formation of the novices, wrote and signed the Circular Letters together with the Servant of God, obtained economic aid from various benefactors and was recognized as superior of the Institute in temporalibus. In 1884 he obtained as a donation to the Institute, from the counts Caracciolo of Piacenza, the vast estate of Gargatano.

Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, witness VIII at the Roman Process, recalls the esteem the sisters had for Fr. Tornatore:

«Fr. Tornatore was held as a father by our sisters, as if he were a cofounder»358.

136. — As the Institute extended, however, and the government became more complex, inconveniences occurred, as Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, recalls:

«As I recalled at the beginning, Mr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, Priest of the Mission, who had had a great part in the foundation of the Institute, habitually lived in the same houses of the Institute, and often followed the foundress and the other sisters who went about visiting the houses. He with much zeal worked for the right running of religious life, but also was often influenced and impressed by those religious who were reproved or punished by the foundress, and often took their side against the very measures of the Servant of God. As is easy to understand, this dualism was a cause of tribulation for the Servant of God, who, with her habitual system, while she did not want to oppose the said Ecclesiastic, in her mind felt well and noted the inconvenience that resulted from it in the discipline of the various communities»359.

The tension culminated in 1888: Fr. Tornatore, aware of being cofounder of the Institute, felt the duty to take part in its government; the Servant of God for her part was advised by authoritative persons to proceed alone in the government, as she writes in her Memoirs360:

«Seized by a strong fear of living always so perplexed (regarding Fr. Tornatore's participation in the government), I went to a learned religious and set out something to him; this began to kindle in me ever more the fear [...]. Again, always with my faithful secretary, I went to consult another General, because the first was also a General. This one calmed me, however, always confirming what the other had said. I begged him to listen well to everything and then I opened myself in everything; and this calmed me indeed, but always disapproving what Fr. Tornatore suggested in the direction. He gave me a method of how I should regulate myself»361.

137. — During the General Chapter of 1888, presided over by the cardinal protector Gaetano Alimonda, Fr. Tornatore was removed from the government of the Institute. His attitude is expressed in a letter of 8 July 1888:

«If [...] I cannot stay in the Institute, my child, without its being divided like the son of the two mothers before Solomon, then I will rather withdraw»362

After 1888, Fr. Tornatore continued to follow from outside and to help the Institute, and the relations between him and the Servant of God remained constant and cordial until his death363

As regards the episode recalled by Fr. Baratelli about Fr. Tornatore's lodging in the generalate house, by which he insinuates ill treatment on the part of the Servant of God, it must on the contrary be noted that that «wretched little room above the church organ» had been chosen by Fr. Tornatore himself, as appears from the letter of the Servant of God to Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, superior of the house364

From all the documents it appears that the Servant of God, in her conduct toward Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, let herself be guided solely by the good of the Institute, by the search for God's will, by obedience to the authoritative counselors to whom she had turned, among them the Servant of God Fr. Bernardino of Portogruaro and Card. Gaetano Alimonda: this demonstrates the rectitude of her intentions and of her conduct.

4. Apostolic Visitation

138. — Various were the motives that caused the Apostolic Visitation, as we have already observed. Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, recalls in his deposition:

«In the Institute of the Servant of God there were, as moreover usually happens in so many others, religious who showed themselves discontented with how they were treated by the superiors, and these, seeing that after making some appeals to the Servant of God they did not have the result they desired, then turned directly to the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, from which they provoked two apostolic visitations. Of the first I have only the news of the fact, and I do not know the particulars, certainly it had no result against the Servant of God [...]. Of the second [...] I recall that Mons. Domenico Serafini, now Assessor of the Holy Office, was appointed visitor. Also of this visitation the result was flattering for the Servant of God, who however had been left most afflicted because such an Apostolic Visitation was a wound to the honor of her Institute. She showed herself, however, of strong and generous spirit in such a contingency, and did not fail to make her own the sentiments of Jonah, saying: ‘If this storm has arisen on my account, set me aside, I beg you; employ me in the humblest offices’. These words she often repeated to the sisters and to me myself she expressed such sentiments several times»365.

139. — The first «Apostolic Visitation» recalled by Card. Granito di Belmonte was not a true and proper Visitation: Mons. Cavicchioni was appointed Delegate, deputed by the Card. Protector to represent him366, and visited only the houses of Rome367.

Another motive of the Apostolic Visitation was the book Travagli e conforti (Labors and Comforts), written by the Servant of God368. To these motives two circumstances are added that cannot be ignored. The first concerns Count Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei, son-in-law of the Servant of God. Fr. Paolino Zavarella writes in his study on the normality of the Servant of God:

«I also wished to investigate how the volume caused troubles and sorrows to the Servant of God, because it was examined by the Holy Office and led to the ‘reponatur’ (sic for dilata) imposed on the Cause [...]. Among other things, the Apostolic Visitor His Excellency Mons. Domenico Serafini, later cardinal, had in hand the volume Travagli e conforti and, while recognizing that it contained nothing condemnable, ordered that it be withdrawn from circulation. Meanwhile the son-in-law of the Servant of God had the volume reach the Holy Office369; he was opposed to the foundress because he demanded from Mother Gattorno large sums which she refused him: hence his gesture of having the volume reach the Holy Office

». The second circumstance concerns Card. Isidoro Verga, Prefect of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars and Protector of the Daughters of St. Anne. Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, observes in this regard:

«The personage to whom I alluded was Cardinal Verga [...]. He had done much good to the Institute. The Servant of God showed herself most grateful to him. Unfortunately it happened that he felt inclined to preferences toward a young religious endowed with fine natural qualities [...]. The anguish of the Servant of God relating to this fact is manifest to me, since she herself spoke to me of it, asking my counsel. That the Servant of God was not mistaken, in not seeing the spirit of the Lord in that fact, so painful to her, appears evident from that religious having, not long after, abandoned the Institute [...]. This fact was also followed by an Apostolic Visitation, but I do not know what relations of cause or effect there are between this and the Visitation»370.

140. — It must not be forgotten, then, that the Apostolic Visitor had been prejudiced against the Servant of God by a penitent of his, Amalia Custo, sister-in-law of the Servant of God371.

In his deposition, Card. Domenico Serafini, witness VI (1st ex officio) at the Roman Process, states:

«The debatable points that I can know about Mother Gattorno, and that I came to know by reason of my mission as Apostolic Visitor, concern external matters, that is, the financial administration of the Institute and her way of governing»372.

As regards the administration, the Visitor observes that the accounts presented to him closed every year with a deficit that was not then carried over to the following year because the Servant of God affirmed that everything was settled, refusing, however, to reveal how it was settled. This attitude of the Servant of God, which aroused much surprise and perhaps irritation in the Apostolic Visitor, is explained by Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process:

«She was most diligent in the administration of the goods of the Institute and other revenues of the Institute [...]. In the administration books the Servant of God, however, abstained, for reasons of humility, from recording some revenues of prodigious origin [...]. She always showed herself deferential to the Apostolic Visitor, although her humility did not permit her to declare the miraculous origin of some revenues»373.

As regards the complaints that came from the houses about the treatment of the sisters, besides what is reported at point 2, Card. Domenico Serafini, witness VI (1st ex officio), declares firmly the rectitude of the Servant of God and the use of the money for the good of the Institute:

«This money that came to Mother Gattorno (from the superiors) was certainly employed for the purpose of maintaining the Institute. In this I am sure that it was not a matter of business dealing, nor to enrich relatives»374.

p. 152

The Apostolic Visitor adds further that if there was anything to complain of it could not be attributed to the Servant of God, whose loyalty he recognizes:

«It seems to me I heard it said that Mother Gattorno, discovering that in some house the sisters suffered because of excessive economy, complained to the respective superiors and protested, demanding that the sisters be treated well. But under the table, by other sisters, other invitations were made to send extraordinary gifts. So it seems to me. However I do not believe that Mother Gattorno ever made two parts, indeed of this I am sure»375.

141. — At the end of the Apostolic Visitation in 1903 (the Servant of God died in 1900), Card. Serafini expressed this positive evaluation in his Report:

«From what has been set forth thus far it can be concluded that the deceased foundress Rosa Gattorno left her Institute solidly established and in a flourishing state on the economic side. After this the undersigned considers it superfluous to dwell now on some irregularities which he found in Gattorno's administration, irregularities which with her death have ceased to exist. Moreover, if Gattorno, being foundress of the Institute and by the prestige she enjoyed over the sisters, believed it lawful to act with a certain freedom and independence in administering the goods of the Institute, goods which in large part she herself had procured for it, the fact has shown that she had at heart the advantage of the Institute above every other thing. The very way in which she, in the last months of her life, secured the patrimony of the Institute against possible claims of whoever might perhaps have dared to claim a part of it, demonstrates the rectitude of her intentions even there where a mother's affection found itself in hard contrast with the duties of a religious superior»376.

The respectful and obedient attitude of the Servant of God toward the Apostolic Visitor is brought into evidence by all the witnesses who speak of the Visitation. Card. Domenico Serafini himself, witness VI (1st ex officio) at the Roman Process, states:

«I was always treated courteously [...]. When I had some sister called from other houses to speak with her, it was never denied me, not even under some pretext; nor can I know that they wished to remove those who were suspected of being opposed to Mother Gattorno»377.

Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, witness VIII at the Roman Process, adds:

«The appearance of the Visitor at Piacenza, where the Servant of God was, was for her a painful blow, and she bore this visit resignedly. Every time the Visitor came to the Servant of God, I saw that she always received him with respect. I recall that the Servant of God, in that time of the Apostolic Visitation, told the sisters to set things before the Visitor with sincerity and truth»378.

142. — The Apostolic Visitation was a painful trial which the Servant of God faced with humility, fully conformed to the will of God and during which her submission and obedience to the Church shone. The Apostolic Visitor dispelled the gravest accusations and proposed measures of slight importance. He also recognized the great rectitude of the Servant of God in her intentions «even there where a mother's affection found itself in hard contrast with the duties of a religious superior».

5. Opposing witnesses

143. — Among the numerous testimonies of the various Processes, very few express negative evaluations of the Servant of God. Of one of them, which concerns a single subject, we have treated in speaking of the question of Fr. Tornatore (cf. 3). Two testimonies remain: that of Sr. A. Ferdinanda Denti and that of Luigia Schenardi.

a) Sr. A. Ferdinanda Denti.

144. — The testimony of Sr. A. Ferdinanda Denti, superior of the house of Lodi, surprises by its contradictions. She begins, in fact, by affirming that she nurtures «great veneration for the Servant of God»; that she desires «that she be declared blessed» and for this end prays to the Lord; she also says she esteems the Servant of God «for the personal experience and knowledge of her, whom in all things I found a person wholly of God»379. Further on, however, she accuses her of having used preferences, of having reproved her because she brought little money, of refusing her a hearing because of relatives.

As regards money, it has already been answered exhaustively in no. 1. It may perhaps be necessary to reiterate that the Servant of God's reminders were directed not at the quantity of the money, but at the administration and at the observance of the vow of poverty380.

As regards partiality and not listening to the sisters because of relatives, this is contested by very numerous other testimonies which bring into evidence the rectitude of the Servant of God. Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi, witness II at the Roman Process, expresses it thus:

«The Servant of God, in assigning to offices, sought the aptitude of the sisters and did not heed qualities that did not relate to the office. She had no preferences for any gift or natural quality, or for the riches that might be hoped to reach the community from any sister. Her intention was directed to God»381.

Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, witness VIII at the Roman Process, explains in her deposition:

«The superiors who came from outside to this house to speak with the Servant of God and hand over to her the surplus of their administration, very often had to wait long before her study because there was always someone of her relatives. Finally, when these had left, they could enter, but they remained very ill at ease because, as was natural, they desired to linger a little with the Servant of God, who instead dispatched them with a certain haste, sending them back to their houses [...]. Gaspare stayed a short time for business. Her brother Checco came often, but for affairs of the Institute, which he himself carried out, and had to stay longer. The sisters, then, who came from outside and who would have wanted the Mother wholly for themselves, were badly impressed if they happened on some bad day because of the relatives' visits and did not stop to distinguish whether Checco or Count Gaspare had come for business. They saw that one succeeded the other, and this jarred on them»382.

To Solenghi's precise explanation must also be added the apprehensiveness of Sr. A. Ferdinanda: returned to her community, she not infrequently had to write to the Mother because she had forgotten the things she had to tell her. It should also be observed that the community of this witness, at that time, was not excessively far from the Mother House, to which she could go fairly easily.

The testimony of Sr. A. Ferdinanda Denti, as has been observed, must be taken with caution, given the contradictions into which she falls, also because the accusations seem prompted by petty feelings of jealousy. This witness then concludes her testimony thus:

«In my judgment in the Servant of God both the theological and the cardinal virtues were resplendent»383.

In these «resplendent virtues» charity and prudence are included.

p. 155

b) Luigia Schenardi 145. — This witness belonged to the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne under the name of Sr. A. Giacomina. She had entered the Institute at the beginning of the foundation, in 1868, and the Servant of God had given her positions of trust, soon making her superior of various communities such as Nizza Monferrato, Ovada, Sestri Ponente and others, and also sending her as Visitor to other houses. She decided to leave the Institute in 1882.

Schenardi shows she has no esteem for the Servant of God; she points out some disorders in the Institute caused, according to the witness, by the excessive indulgence of the Servant of God and by little prudence in government; she also points out that the Servant of God did not provide for the material needs of the Institute and cites as an example the fact that she herself, being in Pisa and in extreme need, the Servant of God did not send her money.

This last fact can be understood bearing in mind that, the Institute being extensive and the needs considerable, the Servant of God did not always have money immediately at hand for emergencies: in these cases she suffered, but wanted the sisters to join her in faith and in trust in Providence and wrest from Heaven the needed help. Indicative in this regard is the episode that occurred to Sr. A. Camilla Valentini: sent as Superior to the house of Bassano del Grappa, she found herself without resources; the Servant of God, consulted, sent her no money but another little orphan to care for, almost to force Providence to assist them, and Providence did indeed arrive, most abundantly384. Not all the daughters were capable of imitating the Servant of God in faith and trust in God.

As regards her leaving the Institute, Schenardi speaks of a harsh letter written by the General Secretary in the name of the Servant of God, on receiving which she decided to leave the Institute, notifying the Servant of God of her decision thus:

«My dearest Mother, I have received your registered letter in which I hear all you say to me, both for my sister and on my own account. In fourteen years that, by great and extraordinary mercy of God, I have been sheltered in the Institute of the Holy Mother, I devoted myself in my nothingness to carrying out as I could, always helped by the goodness of the dear and Holy Mother. The aim of betraying you, Mother, and the Institute I never had, and in the reproaches that they made me several times I always took them as coming from the mouth of God Himself. Now, however, the thing has reached the point of exceeding my weak strength, and I believe God does not permit me to tolerate more, even at the cost of going to eat grass in the fields. I am therefore Judas who betrayed Jesus!

p. 156

I will withdraw from the Institute so as no longer to be the cause of so many ills to you, my dear Mother, but if Judas distrusted forgiveness, I through the merits of Jesus hope for the forgiveness of all my faults. If I alone am the judas, all will be over; because I withdraw at once, and praised be the good God who enlightened them in this, I was not worthy to be a Daughter of St. Anne! I will never forget the good received. I beg you in your goodness to forgive me from your heart the offenses I have done you in the time I was under your protection, and, trusting in your charity for a generous pardon, I ask for the last time your Holy

Blessing while I call myself Sr. A. Giacomina. — The cause of my leaving is not you, Mother, but rather the will of God»385.

Other accusations made by Schenardi against the Servant of God clearly have the flavor of murmuring, and moreover they are isolated accusations. It seems necessary to bear in mind that after many years the witness retains resentment against the Servant of God: this removes serenity and objectivity from the deposition, all the more as this resentment seems caused by her not tolerating that the Servant of God guide and correct her in her office as superior: while she was in Sicily, in fact, she had sent her two visitors.

Despite the accusations, the witness acknowledges that the Servant of God «was a person of charity, taking care of the sick sisters»; «she showed devotion to the Most Holy Eucharist, received Communion every day maintaining an edifying demeanor»; «after Communion she lingered in devout thanksgiving, sometimes for some hours»; «she was sober in the food she took, always meatless».

6. The question of the «Dilata»

146. — In 1932, while the examination of the writings of the Servant of God by the Theological Censors was still under way, the Sacred Congregation of Rites asked the Holy Office for the «Nulla Osta» for the Introduction of the Cause. But that Sacred Congregation replied:

«As to the introduction of the Cause of Beatification of Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne, the same Sacred Congregation has replied: ‘Dilata’»386.

The reasons for the decision were not specified, however.

The reasons, or rather the sole reason for the Dilata, is found expressed in the letter addressed by Mons. Salvatore Natucci to the Holy Father Pius XI, in which he informs the Pontiff:

«During the lifetime of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Daughters of

p. 157

St. Anne, at the insistence of Princess Fitalia of Palermo and with the approval of Card. Guarino, archbishop of Messina, some memoirs written by her were printed. That book, in a visit of Mons. Serafini, Assessor of the Holy Office, to the house of the Daughters of St. Anne in Via Merulana, because of its mysticism was judged dangerous to the young minds of the novices. It was therefore withdrawn from circulation and the existing copies were all collected at the Holy Office. The latter, asked not long ago (as is nowadays done for all Causes) whether the Cause of Gattorno could be introduced, replied negatively. The reason for this reply is the book mentioned above».

In reply to the difficulty raised against the book, Mons. Natucci continues:

«It will be useful, however, to bear in mind: 1) that others, and not the Servant of God, wanted those memoirs printed; 2) that they, before publication, were reviewed and approved by Card. Guarino; 3) that the Theological Censors found nothing in them against faith and morals; 4) that at present they are entirely out of circulation. To whoever considers these circumstances well, the negative reply of the Holy Office cannot fail to seem too grave [...]»387.

Despite this clarification the Holy Office maintained the decision taken for many years and granted the Nulla Osta only in 1979, asking that there be studied

«the normality or otherwise of the Servant of God, with express indication of its nature and its degree in relation to the impairment of personality»388.

147. — The Congregation for the Causes of Saints appointed an Expert in the person of Fr. Paolino Zavarella, Perito in re medica, who submitted his opinion in 1982.

Fr. Zavarella's Opinion is quite complete and detailed. In the conclusion he affirms that the problem raised around the book Travagli e conforti derives from a misunderstanding:

«The study has proved fruitful: it has been possible to ascertain, on the basis of serious and credible documentation, that the whole question that led to the ‘reponatur’ (sic for dilata) arose from a glaring misunderstanding: it was thought that the volume ‘Travagli e conforti etc.’ was the story of a soul, whereas instead it is the story of an Institute, which is quite different. The Servant of God in fact did not wish to write the history of the Institute for two reasons:

a) she did not wish to bring herself into evidence and b) it was repugnant to her to make known the difficulties encountered, so as not to reveal the names of the authors [...].

The solution of the problem is all here: Rosa Gattorno, in the book under discussion, does not speak of herself, but of the Institute: the misunderstanding arose from the fact that the manuscript bore no title and Cardinal Guarino, archbishop of Messina, on his own initiative, gave it the title ‘Travagli e conforti dell'anima nel cammino della perfezione’ (Labors and Comforts of the Soul on the Way of Perfection), a title absolutely improper as Cardinal Granito di Belmonte lamented in his time (Roman Process, Sess. V, fol. 55, vol. I).

The volume, however, contains nothing against faith and morals, on the contrary: in fact it was approved and praised repeatedly by high ecclesiastical authorities.

The misunderstanding having been cleared up, the motive falls that induced the S. Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith to carry out a study on the state of normality or otherwise of the Servant of God [...]. Gattorno's behavior appears always composed, straightforward, marked by a Christian orientation of life, always followed with persevering coherence, with a markedly supernatural vision [...]. Consequently, to the doubt proposed about the normality or otherwise of the Servant of God, I answer that Anna Rosa Gattorno was a person certainly normal from the psychic point of view»389.

p. 158

CHAP. IX
REPUTATION FOR HOLINESS AND MIRACLES

148. — On the platform of a virtuous life carried to heroism, as we have just demonstrated, a reputation for holiness has gone on consolidating which, during the lifetime of the Servant of God, was already most solid and, as we shall now see, giving the word to eyewitnesses, extended to all levels and to the various categories of persons. It was a general and unanimous reputation among all who knew her: Bishops, priests, religious men and women, laity. All recognize that Mother Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne, was a saint, given her constant coherence of virtuous life, her straightforwardness in the path of service to the brethren, her persevering fidelity to the duties of state as daughter of a family, wife, mother, widow and religious, Foundress of a new religious Institute.

On the reputation for holiness of Mother Rosa we have already spoken abundantly throughout the pages of the Informatio and we believe that this reputation remains by now sufficiently proved in the biographical synthesis of the Servant of God and in the collection of the theological and moral virtues woven on the thread of very many eyewitness testimonies of persons who knew Mother Rosa and shared her earthly story.

We now set about proving, on the basis of direct testimonies, the reputation for holiness of the Servant of God herself during life and after death up to the present moment.

p. 159

His Excellency Pietro A. Iorio, witness XVII (2nd ex officio) at the Roman Process, deposes:

«From the first moment in which I knew her, I conceived great esteem for the Servant of God, because I noticed at once the wisdom and prudence with which she was endowed, and that she was not an ordinary woman. Afterwards, having had occasion to deal with her, my esteem for her grew and widened greatly»390

1. Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, gives us this fine synthesis in this regard:

«As to the reputation for holiness of the Servant of God, during her life among us sisters it was that she was a saint worthy of the altars, that she was a worker of graces and miracles. When the sisters came to this house, certainly it was not of the Servant of God that they asked for things she had used, but they well asked it of us in the secretariat in order to make use of them afterwards with devotion, either in cases of illness or for other spiritual needs.

Not only our sisters esteemed her a saint, but all who saw her and conversed with her. I recall a minister plenipotentiary of Bolivia to the French Republic, a certain don Luis Paz, who came to Rome with his whole family and wished to see the Servant of God too. After he had stayed with her, I recall that in the corridor, as he was leaving, he said to us: ‘But what a great woman you have for Mother: you have a saint’.

A certain Mr. Cacace of Taranto founded an orphanage where he called our sisters and established that the care should never be entrusted to others than our sisters; but this did not happen definitively until after he had seen and dealt with the Servant of God, who in him, an atheist, produced a very strong impression. We still preserve a letter written at that time and another afterwards, in which he speaks of his colloquy with our Mother, and there are these expressions, more or less: ‘Those eyes of heaven, that face of a saint, etc.’.

I know of many others, whom I cannot now identify, who held the Servant of God in esteem as a saint, because they themselves said so. After the death of the Servant of God this reputation for holiness not only was maintained among our sisters and outsiders, but grew and grows ever more, so that we cannot rid ourselves of the requests for relics and images of the Servant of God»391.

149. — Princess of Fitalia, Emilia Settimo, witness XXXI at the Roman Process, deposes:

«It is my conviction that the Servant of God was not only a saint, but touched the summit of holiness on a par with the greatest saints, such as St. Teresa, etc. She practiced virtue in the most heroic, the simplest and most natural way.

Penances never prevented her from applying herself with perfection to her office of General, and I do not know whether she ever exceeded in the exercise of the virtues, but I noticed in her a perfect balance in all things»392.

The Princess of Fitalia reaffirms further:

«During her life, the Servant of God was held among the sisters and among outsiders who had known her to be a saint. I know of various persons who came to commend themselves to her prayers, Signora Frascara, the Princess

Lanza di Belmonte, and others. After her death the same esteem as a saint has lasted among the sisters and I believe also among outsiders. I, who commend myself to the Servant of God in every circumstance, small and great, of my life, continually experience her patronage, and count on it, she having explicitly promised to help me always. This is my great comfort in all the contingencies of my life, it lightens everything for me, gives me confidence and support»393.

Fr. Gioacchino Corrado, witness XXXIII at the Roman Process, declares:

«I have great admiration for the Servant of God, and from the time I knew her, I foresaw how it would end, and how one day the Process of Beatification would begin»394.

Card. Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, made this fine declaration:

«In the circle in which she lived and in her relations, the Servant of God I esteemed and she was esteemed by others as a woman of extraordinary virtue, and such esteem has been preserved after her death to this day, spreading ever more. And this esteem I must note was not produced by any artifice. I note further that of the persons who esteemed the Servant of God, there were not and there are not only those easy to esteem and to believe, but also very serious and authoritative persons. I for my part judge the virtue of the Servant of God to be that of a saint, and I hope that this my judgment will be confirmed by God with miracles of the first order through the intercession of His Servant»395.

Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi, witness XL at the Roman Process, attests:

«The Servant of God enjoyed a reputation for holiness during her life. And this reputation for holiness was founded precisely on the virtues that shone in her, on the extraordinary gifts conferred on her by the Lord [...]. And I also know that even outside the Institute she enjoyed among various persons, for the same reasons, esteem for holiness»396.

The same witness adds further:

«The reputation and opinion of holiness of the Servant of God both among the sisters and among outsiders did not lessen with her death, but grew, and this not by any artifice, but through her virtues and the graces with which, as the sisters and some outsider told me, she has been illustrated after her death. Among others who esteemed her so much, I shall recall also the Archbishop of Siena Mons. Pierallini who spoke of her with great reverence as of a saint; likewise Mons. Alberti, his vicar general. Likewise Mons. Capponi, archbishop of Pisa, spoke of her as a great soul»397.

Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, attests:

«When the Servant of God died, all our sisters, as far as I know, said: ‘A saint has died’, and I always understood that they meant saint of the altar. Among persons outside the Institute one heard everyone say: ‘A great woman has died; a saint has died’; and this was so universally repeated that Mons. Vincenzo Sardi advised us to collect together all the voices, both for and against. The same advice was given us by Mons. Achille Martini, advocate of the saints, although he had spoken only once with the Servant of God. The Cardinal Protector, Rampolla, on the occasion of the introduction of the ordinary Process, showed himself wholly favorable and, in my presence, said to Mother Carrega: ‘It is rather a duty’.

This reputation for holiness has not faded with the years, but has increased, as appeared especially on the occasion of the first fiftieth anniversary of the foundation of the Institute. Then we received not only from our sisters, but also from lay persons and from bishops letters extolling the virtues of the Servant of God and expressing wishes that she soon be raised to the honors of the altars»398.

150. — Mr. Tommaso Monti, witness XI at the Roman Process, expresses himself in these terms:

«I have always esteemed, after having dealt with her at length, the Servant of God a woman of no common virtue, as I deduced from the facts of the growth of her Institute and from her conduct in handling affairs. I would not even exclude that she was worthy of the honor of the altars, but I have no particular facts to allege in support of this my impression; and I also have the impression that one day she may be on the altars, because for the long time I was near her, I always knew her as a woman of superior virtue»399.

Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV at the Roman Process, has left us this her testimony:

«I heard many times Cardinal Verga, speaking of the Servant of God, call her ‘your holy Mother General’; Cardinal Pende, Mons. Chappon bishop of Nice, Abbot Fante, Canon Tosti of Foligno, and others, I heard speak of the Servant of God during her life as of a saint. I also heard people of the common folk speak of the Servant of God as of a saint. When she went on visitation to Palermo, I know they wanted to kiss even her feet. Several chaplains of our houses, as for example of Borgo S. Donnino, of Caltanissetta, said: ‘Your Mother is certainly a saint, because when she has made a visit to your houses, one sees the traces’. The esteem and veneration for the Servant of God after her death not only has been preserved, but has also grown because one sees that she is not invoked in vain. Many are interested in the Process, ask whether it has begun, like the countess Di Nunzio Maria dei Malatesta.

In the whole Institute, both during life and after death, also among the sisters who never knew her, the esteem and veneration that has always been held toward the Servant of God is as for a saint and, to give the expression I heard, ‘niche-worthy’ (that is, worthy of the altar); and this esteem, both in the Institute and outside, had its basis and origin in the knowledge of the virtues of the Servant of God, knowledge had directly, or by means of her works, or from those persons who came fully close to her. And I believe that this esteem is truly just and due»400.

Proof of the reputation for holiness enjoyed by the Servant of God in life and after death is also the following episode, of which her brother Federico was the protagonist, a follower of Garibaldi and of Mazzini, known for his anticlericalism, which, however, did not prevent him from nurturing a sincere esteem and veneration for his sister. Taunted in the Chamber in 1907 by Hon. Santini as «the steward of the nuns of Via Merulana», he replied proclaiming the holiness of life of his sister:

«Yes, I had a sister who was a nun, but notwithstanding this I have kept my principles intact against clericalism and against Catholics. So no charge should be made against me for having had a sister who was a nun, who for the rest was a holy woman»401.

151. — In 1941, on the occasion of the anniversary of the foundation of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Fr. A. M. Fiocchi, a Jesuit, published the biography of Mother Rosa in two volumes, entitled: La Serva di Dio Rosa Gattorno, Fondatrice delle Figlie di S. Anna (The Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne). At the end of the second volume, the author concludes his work with these words, which we record here as proof of the permanent and ever living reputation for holiness of the Servant of God:

«On 27 July 1912 the Ordinary informative Process was begun in Rome on the reputation for holiness, the virtues and the miracles (of Mother Rosa); the very long Process lasted fully 15 years, occupying 444 sessions, and closed on 26 January 1927. Other informative processes were meanwhile held in Genoa, Piacenza, Naples, Palermo: the complete file has the conspicuous bulk of 8000 pages of protocol [...].

Much has been said in these forty years of prodigious graces obtained from God through the intercession of Mother Rosa Gattorno, and several are recounted in the processes mentioned. Indeed some are accompanied by juridical testimonies, but this is not the place to narrate them, both because they would form an almost infinite series, and especially for the due discretion before the authority of the Church, which on those facts has not yet pronounced its judgment.

One event, however, we cannot and must not pass over in silence; and it is the living fruit of the work of Mother Gattorno. The divine Savior said that the tree is known by its fruits: well, the work founded by this generous woman bears manifest the seal of God who inspired and helped it. At her death it was already grandiose [...]: today, on the anniversary of the foundation of the Daughters of St. Anne, those figures show conspicuous increases and attest the constant flourishing of the Institute founded by Mother Gattorno!402.

The sisters number fully 8,120, that is, 7,827 professed, 215 novices and 78 postulants. The war has thinned the number of new vocations a little; but it is a passing phenomenon. The houses are 405, that is: 327 in Italy and 78 abroad; several of these are in mission territory. The novitiates are 4 in Italy and 4 abroad [...]. This blessed tree, so leafy and fruitful, has its roots in the heart of Rosa Gattorno, a Mother therefore in every way admirable and honored by her own offspring in the Church of Christ: ‘Quasi mater honorificata’»403.

When in 1912 the Processes of beatification of Mother Rosa were begun, many persons of prominence in the ecclesiastical world wrote laudatory letters to the Superiors of the Institute, highlighting the timeliness of the Cause and the exceptional virtues and reputation for holiness of the Servant of God. From the chorus of so many voices we choose, by way of example, the following:

Mons. Valerio, archbishop of Salerno:

«I remember the deceased well, and on the occasions when I visited her in Rome, I always carried away the most pleasing impression, reading on her face and in her speech that wealth of virtues with which her heart and her soul were adorned. I therefore pray, for the glory of God and for the reward due to the just, that the Cause for her Beatification may go well forward and soon»404

4. Mons. Zuccaro, bishop:

«I pray the Lord that He may bless the wishes of so many beautiful souls, who certainly seek the glory of God in wanting the Servant of God exalted to the honor of the altars. I had the pleasure of knowing her and of conferring with her, when by word of mouth, or by letters she urged me to the spread of the Institute in this island (Sicily), and on this subject were our conversations, which, thanks be to God, had their beneficial fruits»405.

p. 164

Mons. Domenico Gaspare, archbishop of Monreale:

«I, who had the good fortune to know her (Mother Rosa) and to approach her more than once, in those pieces of news read (the articles), had to recall with satisfaction her humility, her sweetness in speaking, her prudence in discussing and in the resolutions to be taken. I assure you that I am truly glad and moved. And if the Lord in His mercy will grant me still some further day of life, I shall wish to follow such process with interest with the sweet hope of seeing and venerating her, if possible, before I die, on the altars»406.

Mons. Ambrogio Luddi, bishop of Assisi:

«From the first time I knew Mother Sr. Rosa Gattorno, foundress of her Institute, I carried away a pleasing and sweet impression, because in her everything bore holiness and veneration. Her gaze, her words, her sentiments, her composure, her cheerfulness with the appearance of a mortified life, her love for her daughters, her zeal for the salvation of souls, her ardor for the growth of her beneficent work and the array of wise views that so distinguished her, everything gave a glimpse of the beauty of her soul and said eloquently that she was more of heaven than of earth. Nor did this impression of mine, while the dear Mother lived, ever diminish in me, but rather went on intensifying as the brief mutual conversations were repeated: so that the last time I saw her she seemed to me more admirable and venerable than ever; perhaps because she was near to completing her great sacrifice»407.

152. — Let us hear, last, the voice of Canon Mons. Silvio Ceccatelli, of Prato, who recalls with gratitude the wise and prudent help received from Mother Rosa at very significant moments of his life:

«Twice I had occasion to write to that holy woman. The first, when, by order of my superiors, I was obliged to assume the spiritual direction of the Daughters of St. Anne of Prato. I recall that the moment was not propitious for me who, young and new to such directions, had to enter on fulfilling a most sacred duty in a religious community that no longer enjoyed the esteem of the people of Prato because of some inconveniences that had occurred and become public knowledge. If I accepted the burdensome office, it was out of obedience to my superiors; but if I set myself with intelligence of love and with zeal to try to do a little good to the house of Prato and to the new spiritual daughters, I owe it to Sr. Rosa Gattorno. She replied to me under date of November 1892: ‘[...] I too understand the position of that house [...] and I pray Heaven to reward her for me’ [...]. And her prayer was effective enough, for in a short time I was rewarded in seeing peace and zeal return to this house, and the esteem for these sisters increase every day more. Moreover I believe it was her prayers, if, even amid sorrows, I received great comforts and rewards from my superiors.

The second time in which I turned to so good and holy a Mother was on

p. 165

5 December 1892, to make known to her my thought of establishing the Little Educatory of St. Anne for abandoned childhood and the Leo XIII Educatory for little girls preparing for First Communion. Regarding these institutions I was somewhat opposed by some who seemed to me friends, and perhaps I would have abandoned the idea, had I not had the approval and encouragement of Mother Gattorno, who said to me: ‘[...] I am very glad to tell you that not only do I approve what you have established regarding that house; indeed it gives me much pleasure that the matter has been so arranged [...]. Meanwhile I shall busy myself to obtain for you the blessing of the Holy Father, so that the work may succeed even better’ [...].

Thus with her approval and encouragement and with the blessing of the Holy Father, in January 1893 the Educatory was solemnly inaugurated, which today receives so many poor little girls and has the sympathies of the citizens and of the authorities; and all this material and spiritual growth I attribute entirely to the prayers and to the prudent and charitable cooperation of the Servant of God Sr. Rosa Gattorno, who, I am certain, today from heaven continues her protection over all her daughters»408.

CONCLUSION

LORDS CARDINALS, MOST REV. CONSULTORS,

153. — From all that has been set forth in this Informatio, on the sure and solid ground of the Informative Sources (testimonial, documentary and biographical), some conclusions can be drawn, which are nothing other than the concentrate of what has been written.

There existed around the person of Mother Rosa Gattorno, already during her earthly life, a wide reputation for holiness of life and extraordinary virtues, which then burst forth in a very striking manner on the occasion of the solemn funeral and is persistent and alive down to our own days. At a distance of more than ninety years from the completion of her earthly career, today one is in a position to decipher more clearly the divine origin of this reputation, to evaluate its nature and foundation, resting not on transitory expressions of enthusiasm, in a socio-human context prone to suggestion, but on an authentic fabric of life, of good works and of conduct that attracted the attention and admiration of disparate social categories.

Convinced of the reputation for holiness of the Servant of God, Fr. Lázaro Iriarte expresses himself thus in the introduction to his study on the Spiritual Physiognomy of Mother Rosa:

«I must confess that, finding myself before the mass of the writings of the Servant of God, the problems raised around her Cause of Canonization and the complexity of the manifestations of her spirituality, in certain aspects truly disconcerting, I remained somewhat perplexed.

As I advanced, however, in the analytical reading of the rich testimony of herself left in her Memoirs and in her book Travagli e conforti, I saw her spiritual and apostolic figure grow. This image then offered itself to me in all its evangelical dimension on comparing the results of my study with the hundreds of cards drawn from the letters of the Foundress [...].

If we had as a source of information only the external testimony of the depositions of the witnesses who were heard in the various ordinary processes, everything would have been easy; in fact, the fortunate foundress, as her contemporaries saw her, especially her spiritual daughters and the various personalities who dealt with her intimately, appears as a soul of high union with God, of intrepid faith, full of charity and sacrifice, of goodness, of humility, most penitent, adorned with charismatic gifts of every kind. But it was precisely the image of herself traced by her in her writings, concretely in the book Travagli e conforti, that gave rise to the Dilata of the Holy Office, when in 1932 the Congregation of Rites asked for the nulla osta for the introduction of the Cause. In 1979 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (formerly the Holy Office) granted the nulla osta, asking however that there be studied ‘the state of normality or otherwise’409 of the Servant of God. Then the Congregation for the Causes of Saints thought a medical-psychic expert opinion necessary.

Fr. Paolino Zavarella, doctor of medicine, with his most weighty and exhaustive ‘opinion’410, came to dispel definitively every shadow of uncertainty: Rosa Gattorno was a woman not only fully normal from the psychic point of view, but endowed with a notable intellectual and volitional balance, as also with extraordinary practical sense, enterprising initiative and ease in human relations; qualities which, elevated and enriched by supernatural gifts, won her the esteem and veneration of prominent civil and ecclesiastical personalities»411.

154. — From what we have set forth, the behavioral picture of Mother Rosa turns out to be of a truly superior spiritual and moral stature. Unsurpassable she was seen in the exercise of charity, with all the surrounding spirit of sacrifice and dedication with the marks of heroic generosity and perseverance. In a thorough examination of the life, works and conduct of the Servant of God we have been able to verify that her reputation for holiness not only corresponded to the truth, but there could also be found in her a set of very exceptional Virtues which gave precisely to those who dealt with her the conviction of finding themselves before a woman and a religious who lived by Faith, Hope, Charity in a framework of moral virtues and in a context of true and convinced following of Christ poor, chaste, obedient, humble.

p. 167

At the end, therefore, of the examination of the whole behavioral picture of Mother Rosa Gattorno as a young girl in the family, as wife, as mother, as widow and then, finally, as foundress and as religious superior general, the final and overall judgment should be none other than positive and favorable: the Servant of God was a heroine in the exercise of all the virtues.

MOST EMINENT CARDINALS AND BISHOPS, MOST REV. CONSULTORS,

155. — In entrusting to Your authoritative judgment the holy life and heroic virtues of the Servant of God Mother Rosa Gattorno, foundress of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, we at the same time hand You the suppliant prayer that You may be able to cast a favorable vote unanimously. This petition is made not only by the undersigned Relator and Postulator, but by the whole noble Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne — which with good reason can boast of such and so great a Mother Foundress — and by the numerous faithful who have always and devoutly believed in the holiness of Mother Rosa, awaiting nothing else than to be able to venerate her in the glory of the altars.
